title: On this day in New Zealand politics
description: One to three dated events from New Zealand political and constitutional history for every day of the year, written in plain English for the Ballot Book NZ voter guide.

01-01.title: Parliament becomes a single chamber
01-01.text: The Legislative Council, New Zealand's appointed upper house, ceased to exist on this day. Since then Parliament has had only one chamber, the House of Representatives.

01-01.title: Constitution Act comes into force
01-01.text: The Constitution Act 1986 took effect. It brought together the main rules on the Sovereign, the Governor-General, Parliament and the courts, and ended the United Kingdom's power to make laws for New Zealand.

01-01.title: Supreme Court of New Zealand established
01-01.text: New Zealand's own final court of appeal came into being, replacing appeals to the Privy Council in London. It heard its first case on 1 July 2004.

01-02.title: Provinces abolished
01-02.text: New Zealand's provincial governments formally ceased to exist, leaving a single central Parliament and local councils. The Abolition of Provinces Act had been passed in 1875.
01-02.note: No political event found for 2 January; nearest is 1 January 1877.

01-03.title: Survey ship arrives for Wellington settlement
01-03.text: The New Zealand Company's survey ship Cuba reached Port Nicholson (Wellington) to prepare for organised British settlement, weeks before the Treaty of Waitangi was signed.

01-04.title: Māori electorates vote in the 1875-76 election
01-04.text: Polling in the four Māori electorates was held on 4 and 15 January 1876, as part of a general election spread over several weeks.

01-05.title: Bastion Point occupation begins
01-05.text: Ngāti Whātua and supporters began occupying Takaparawhau (Bastion Point) in Auckland to stop a housing development on former tribal land. The occupation lasted 506 days.

01-06.title: George Grey wins the Thames seat
01-06.text: Former governor Sir George Grey topped the poll in Thames during the 1875-76 general election. He became premier in 1877.

01-06.title: Birth of Norman Kirk
01-06.text: Norman Kirk, who led Labour to victory in 1972 and died in office in 1974, was born in Waimate.

01-07.title: Northern Maori MP dies
01-07.text: Tāpihana Paikea, Labour MP for Northern Maori, died. Matiu Rata won the by-election in March and later founded Mana Motuhake.

01-07.title: Death of Jim Anderton
01-07.text: Jim Anderton, founder of NewLabour, the Alliance and the Progressive Party and deputy prime minister from 1999 to 2002, died aged 79.

01-08.title: Southern Maori MP dies in office
01-08.text: Taare Parata, the Liberal MP for Southern Maori, died, leading to a by-election in the seat later that year.

01-09.title: Birth of Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan
01-09.text: Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan, MP for Southern Maori from 1967 to 1996 and the first Māori woman to serve as a Cabinet minister, was born.

01-09.title: Former Speaker Stan Whitehead dies
01-09.text: Sir Stanley Whitehead, Labour MP for Nelson and a former Speaker, died in office, forcing a by-election in Nelson.

01-10.title: Social Credit Political League founded
01-10.text: The Social Credit Political League was set up, growing out of an earlier monetary-reform movement. It won its first seat in 1966 and became the main third party of the 1970s and early 1980s.

01-10.title: Waikato-Tainui files Tribunal claim over section 7AA
01-10.text: The iwi lodged a Waitangi Tribunal claim challenging the Government's plan to repeal section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act.

01-11.title: New Zealand coat of arms gazetted
01-11.text: The royal warrant granting New Zealand its own coat of arms was published in the New Zealand Gazette.

01-12.title: The Queen opens Parliament in person
01-12.text: Queen Elizabeth II opened a special session of Parliament in Wellington during her first tour, the first time a reigning monarch had done so in New Zealand.

01-13.title: Birth of the Māori Queen
01-13.text: Ngā Wai hono i te pō, who became Māori Queen in 2024 as head of the Kīngitanga, was born.

01-13.title: Trade deal with the United Arab Emirates signed
01-13.text: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Trade Minister Todd McClay signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement with the United Arab Emirates.

01-14.title: Hobson sworn in as Lieutenant-Governor
01-14.text: William Hobson took his oath as Lieutenant-Governor of New Zealand in Sydney before sailing to the Bay of Islands to seek a treaty with Māori chiefs.

01-15.title: Māori electorates vote in the 1871 election
01-15.text: Elections in the four Māori electorates were held on 1 and 15 January 1871, during the general election for the 5th Parliament.

01-15.title: Kim Dotcom announces the Internet Party
01-15.text: Internet entrepreneur Kim Dotcom announced he would form a political party. The Internet Party later allied with Mana for the 2014 election.

01-16.title: First woman mayor in the British Empire
01-16.text: Elizabeth Yates was sworn in as Mayor of Onehunga, the first woman to hold a mayoralty anywhere in the British Empire.

01-16.title: Independent Electoral Review reports
01-16.text: The Ministry of Justice published the final report of the Independent Electoral Review, which recommended changes such as lowering the party-vote threshold.

01-17.title: Walter Nash becomes Labour leader
01-17.text: Walter Nash became Leader of the Opposition after the death of Peter Fraser. He led Labour back into government in 1957.

01-18.title: Supreme Court building opened
01-18.text: Prince William formally opened the new Supreme Court building in Wellington.

01-19.title: Jacinda Ardern announces her resignation
01-19.text: Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced she would step down as Labour leader and prime minister, saying she no longer had enough in the tank.

01-20.title: Governor Jervois takes office
01-20.text: Sir William Jervois became Governor of New Zealand. Governors at this time still played a real part in politics.

01-21.title: Atkinson's last-minute appointments
01-21.text: Outgoing Premier Harry Atkinson arranged appointments to the Legislative Council around 20-22 January 1891, days before the Liberals took office. Critics said it stacked the upper house.

01-22.title: First New Zealand Company settlers arrive
01-22.text: The Aurora, the first New Zealand Company ship carrying immigrants, arrived at Port Nicholson (Wellington).

01-22.title: Chris Hipkins confirmed as Labour leader
01-22.text: The Labour caucus confirmed Chris Hipkins as party leader, making him prime minister-designate after Jacinda Ardern's resignation.

01-23.title: Parliament meets to decide who governs
01-23.text: The 11th Parliament opened after the 1890 election. The next day the Liberals under John Ballance took office.

01-24.title: First Liberal government takes office
01-24.text: John Ballance's Liberal ministry took office. It is usually counted as New Zealand's first organised party government and stayed in power until 1912.

01-25.title: Birth of T. W. Rātana
01-25.text: Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana, founder of the Rātana movement, was born. His birthday is still marked each year at Rātana Pā, where political leaders gather before Waitangi Day.

01-25.title: Chris Hipkins sworn in as prime minister
01-25.text: Chris Hipkins was sworn in as New Zealand's 41st prime minister, with Carmel Sepuloni as deputy prime minister, the first person of Pacific descent in that role.

01-26.title: 'Teapot tape' leaked
01-26.text: A recording of a 2011 campaign conversation between John Key and ACT's John Banks, made in an Auckland cafe, was published online after months of legal argument.

01-26.title: Plan to lower voting age dropped
01-26.text: The Government confirmed it would not continue the previous government's bill to lower the voting age for local elections to 16.

01-27.title: Raf Manji becomes TOP leader
01-27.text: Former Christchurch city councillor Raf Manji was named leader of The Opportunities Party.

01-28.title: Peter Dunne returns as a minister
01-28.text: Peter Dunne was reappointed to the Executive as Minister of Internal Affairs, months after resigning over a leak inquiry.

01-28.title: Election date announced
01-28.text: Jacinda Ardern announced that the 2020 general election would be held on 19 September. It was later postponed to 17 October because of COVID-19.

01-29.title: Hobson arrives in the Bay of Islands
01-29.text: Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson reached the Bay of Islands aboard HMS Herald, eight days before the Treaty of Waitangi was signed.

01-30.title: Hobson reads his proclamations
01-30.text: At Kororāreka (Russell) Hobson read proclamations announcing his authority and that land purchases from Māori would need Crown approval.

01-30.title: Mike Sabin resigns, triggering Northland by-election
01-30.text: National MP Mike Sabin resigned from Parliament. Winston Peters won the resulting Northland by-election in March.

01-30.title: Taranaki Maunga redress law passed
01-30.text: Parliament passed the Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act, giving the mountain legal personhood and settling Treaty claims.

01-31.title: Wage order before the waterfront dispute
01-31.text: The Arbitration Court issued a general wage order raising wages 15 percent. Watersiders' demands for the same rise helped trigger the 1951 waterfront dispute.

02-01.title: Move to end Māori ward polls announced
02-01.text: Local Government Minister Nanaia Mahuta announced a bill to remove the rules letting a public poll overturn a council's decision to set up Māori wards.

02-02.title: Bridges rules out New Zealand First
02-02.text: National leader Simon Bridges said National would not form a coalition with New Zealand First after the 2020 election.

02-03.title: Government approves first COVID-19 vaccine
02-03.text: The Government formally approved the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine for use in New Zealand.

02-04.title: Death of Tohu Kākahi
02-04.text: Tohu Kākahi, one of the two prophet leaders of the Parihaka community in Taranaki, died.

02-04.title: USS Buchanan turned away
02-04.text: The Lange government declined a visit by the US warship USS Buchanan because the United States would not say whether it carried nuclear weapons. The decision strained the ANZUS alliance.

02-04.title: Trans-Pacific Partnership signed in Auckland
02-04.text: Trade ministers from twelve countries signed the TPP agreement at SkyCity in Auckland, amid protests outside.

02-05.title: Chiefs debate the Treaty at Waitangi
02-05.text: Hobson met Māori chiefs at James Busby's house at Waitangi, where the proposed treaty was read out and debated for hours.

02-06.title: Treaty of Waitangi signed
02-06.text: About 40 chiefs signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi at Waitangi with William Hobson for the Crown. Copies were later taken around the country for more signatures.

02-06.title: Waitangi Treaty grounds gifted to the nation
02-06.text: Governor-General Lord Bledisloe's gift of the Treaty House and grounds at Waitangi was formally marked at a large gathering.

02-06.title: First New Zealand Day holiday
02-06.text: 6 February became a national public holiday for the first time, under the New Zealand Day Act 1973. It was renamed Waitangi Day in 1976.

02-07.title: Holyoake steps down; Marshall becomes PM
02-07.text: Keith Holyoake resigned after more than eleven years as prime minister. Jack Marshall succeeded him, but lost the election later that year.

02-07.title: ACT launches Treaty Principles Bill campaign
02-07.text: ACT began a public campaign for its Treaty Principles Bill, which aimed to define the Treaty's principles in law.

02-08.title: MP killed in the Taranaki war
02-08.text: Thomas King, MP for Grey and Bell, was killed during fighting in Taranaki. Harry Atkinson, a future premier, took the seat.

02-08.title: Kiwi Party deregistered
02-08.text: The Kiwi Party asked to be deregistered and merged into the Conservative Party.

02-08.title: Convoy protest arrives at Parliament
02-08.text: A convoy of vehicles protesting against COVID-19 vaccine mandates reached Parliament, starting an occupation of its grounds that lasted 23 days.

02-09.title: Marshall ministry takes office
02-09.text: The ministers of Jack Marshall's new government were sworn in, two days after Keith Holyoake stepped down.

02-10.title: Plan to replace the Resource Management Act
02-10.text: The Government confirmed the Resource Management Act 1991 would be replaced by three new laws. The replacement Acts were repealed by the next government.

02-10.title: Police try to clear Parliament protest
02-10.text: Police arrested more than 120 people in an attempt to end the occupation of Parliament's grounds. The protest continued until 2 March.

02-11.title: Donna Awatere Huata suspended from ACT caucus
02-11.text: ACT suspended list MP Donna Awatere Huata after fraud allegations. She was later expelled from Parliament under party-hopping law.

02-12.title: Wellington North by-election
02-12.text: The Reform candidate held Wellington North in a wartime by-election, but a strong Labour showing alarmed the governing coalition.

02-12.title: Apology for the Chinese poll tax
02-12.text: Prime Minister Helen Clark formally apologised to Chinese New Zealanders for the poll tax imposed on Chinese immigrants from 1881.

02-12.title: NZ First MP Brian Donnelly resigns
02-12.text: Brian Donnelly left Parliament to become High Commissioner to the Cook Islands and was replaced by the next person on the New Zealand First list.

02-13.title: Waterfront dispute begins
02-13.text: The 1951 waterfront dispute began when watersiders refused to work overtime and employers locked them out. It lasted 151 days and the Holland government used emergency powers against the union.

02-13.title: MMP review opens for submissions
02-13.text: The Electoral Commission released a consultation paper for its review of MMP, triggered by the 2011 referendum result.

02-13.title: Bill English announces resignation
02-13.text: Former prime minister Bill English announced he would step down as National Party leader and leave Parliament.

02-14.title: Auckland put into level 3 lockdown
02-14.text: After new community COVID-19 cases in Papatoetoe, the Government moved Auckland to alert level 3 and the rest of the country to level 2.

02-14.title: National emergency declared for Cyclone Gabrielle
02-14.text: The Government declared a national state of emergency, only the third in New Zealand's history, as Cyclone Gabrielle hit the North Island.

02-15.title: Vogel's second ministry formed
02-15.text: Julius Vogel returned as premier, replacing Daniel Pollen's ministry.

02-15.title: Conversion practices ban passed
02-15.text: Parliament passed the Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Act with broad cross-party support, banning so-called conversion therapy.

02-16.title: Taito Phillip Field quits Labour
02-16.text: Mangere MP Taito Phillip Field left the Labour Party after being threatened with expulsion. He later founded the New Zealand Pacific Party.

02-17.title: Electoral Finance Act repealed
02-17.text: Parliament repealed the Electoral Finance Act 2007 by 112 votes to 9. Only the Greens opposed the repeal.

02-17.title: Pike River agency ends plan to go further into mine
02-17.text: The Pike River Recovery Agency abandoned plans to go beyond a rockfall in the mine, after a long political campaign by the families of the 29 men killed in 2010.

02-18.title: Akaroa MP resigns
02-18.text: Robert Heaton Rhodes resigned as MP for Akaroa, leading to a by-election won by William Montgomery.

02-18.title: New Zealand's last execution
02-18.text: Walter Bolton was hanged for murder, the last person executed in New Zealand. The death penalty for murder was abolished in 1961.

02-18.title: Social Credit wins Rangitikei by-election
02-18.text: Bruce Beetham won the Rangitikei by-election, giving Social Credit a seat in Parliament for the first time since 1969.

02-19.title: Prostitution Reform Bill passes second reading
02-19.text: The bill to decriminalise sex work passed its second reading 62 votes to 56. It became law by a single vote in June.

02-19.title: Jami-Lee Ross charged over donations
02-19.text: Former National MP Jami-Lee Ross was named as one of four people charged by the Serious Fraud Office over donations to the National Party. He was later acquitted.

02-19.title: NZ First and Green MPs clash over Ukraine
02-19.text: New Zealand First MPs criticised Green MP Ricardo Menéndez March over comments on the war in Ukraine, in one of several rows between the two parties that year.

02-20.title: Lianne Dalziel resigns from Cabinet
02-20.text: Immigration Minister Lianne Dalziel resigned after misleading the public about a leaked document. She returned as a minister after the 2005 election.

02-20.title: Grant Robertson announces retirement
02-20.text: Former finance minister Grant Robertson announced he would leave Parliament to become Vice-Chancellor of the University of Otago.

02-21.title: Governor Normanby leaves office
02-21.text: The Marquess of Normanby ended his term as Governor of New Zealand.

02-21.title: Death of Green MP Efeso Collins
02-21.text: Green list MP Fa'anānā Efeso Collins died suddenly during a charity event in Auckland. He had entered Parliament only months earlier.

02-21.title: Andrew Bayly resigns as minister
02-21.text: Andrew Bayly resigned from his ministerial roles after an incident involving a staff member.

02-22.title: Newall becomes Governor-General
02-22.text: Sir Cyril Newall was sworn in as Governor-General, serving through most of the Second World War.

02-22.title: Christchurch earthquake
02-22.text: A magnitude 6.3 earthquake killed 185 people in Christchurch. The Government later set up the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority with special powers.

02-23.title: Parliament opens in the Depression
02-23.text: The 24th Parliament opened, with the United-Reform coalition in power during the worst of the Great Depression.

02-24.title: Māori wards law passes under urgency
02-24.text: Parliament passed the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act, removing the right to force a local poll on Māori wards. It received royal assent on 1 March.

02-25.title: Governor Onslow leaves office
02-25.text: The Earl of Onslow ended his term as Governor. His successor, Lord Glasgow, later signed the women's suffrage law.

02-25.title: Mount Albert by-election
02-25.text: Jacinda Ardern won the Mount Albert by-election for Labour after Prime Minister-turned-diplomat David Shearer resigned the seat.

02-26.title: Birth of Helen Clark
02-26.text: Helen Clark, prime minister from 1999 to 2008 and later head of the UN Development Programme, was born in Hamilton.

02-27.title: Simon Bridges elected National leader
02-27.text: National MPs chose Simon Bridges to replace Bill English as party leader and Leader of the Opposition.

02-27.title: Tabuteau becomes NZ First deputy
02-27.text: Fletcher Tabuteau replaced Ron Mark as deputy leader of New Zealand First.

02-28.title: United New Zealand joins the Bolger government
02-28.text: Peter Dunne became a minister as his United party entered a coalition with National, keeping the government's majority ahead of the first MMP election.

02-28.title: First COVID-19 case in New Zealand
02-28.text: New Zealand confirmed its first case of COVID-19, in a person who had returned from Iran.

02-28.title: Smokefree generation law repealed
02-28.text: Parliament repealed the previous government's smokefree laws, which would have banned tobacco sales to people born after 2008.

02-29.title: Tribunal hears urgent Māori Health Authority claim
02-29.text: The Waitangi Tribunal held an urgent hearing on 29 February and 1 March on the Government's plan to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority.

03-01.title: Lange debates nuclear weapons at Oxford
03-01.text: Prime Minister David Lange argued at the Oxford Union that nuclear weapons are morally indefensible, a famous moment in New Zealand's nuclear-free stance.

03-01.title: Māori wards Act receives royal assent
03-01.text: The Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021 became law, removing binding polls on Māori wards.

03-02.title: Police clear Parliament grounds occupation
03-02.text: Police ended the 23-day protest occupation of Parliament's grounds against COVID-19 mandates, in a day of clashes and fires.

03-03.title: Fox returns as premier for a fourth time
03-03.text: William Fox formed his fourth and shortest ministry, lasting until April.

03-03.title: Margaret Wilson becomes first woman Speaker
03-03.text: Labour's Margaret Wilson was elected Speaker of the House, the first woman to hold the office.

03-04.title: Duncan MacIntyre becomes deputy prime minister
03-04.text: Duncan MacIntyre took over as deputy prime minister from Brian Talboys in the Muldoon government.

03-05.title: Botany by-election
03-05.text: Jami-Lee Ross won the Botany by-election for National after Pansy Wong resigned over misuse of travel perks.

03-06.title: The Opportunities Party registered
03-06.text: The Electoral Commission registered The Opportunities Party, founded by economist Gareth Morgan.

03-07.title: Ardern becomes Labour deputy leader
03-07.text: Jacinda Ardern replaced Annette King as deputy leader of the Labour Party, five months before becoming leader.

03-08.title: CPTPP signed
03-08.text: New Zealand signed the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership in Santiago, Chile, after the United States had withdrawn from the earlier TPP.

03-09.title: Referendum on pub closing hours
03-09.text: Voters decided in a referendum to keep six o'clock closing for pubs, by about three to one.

03-09.title: Russia Sanctions Act passed unanimously
03-09.text: Parliament passed the Russia Sanctions Act in one day in response to the invasion of Ukraine, letting New Zealand impose sanctions without a UN mandate.

03-10.title: Birth of Kate Sheppard
03-10.text: Kate Sheppard, leader of the campaign that won New Zealand women the vote in 1893, was born in Liverpool, England.

03-10.title: Chlöe Swarbrick elected Green co-leader
03-10.text: Chlöe Swarbrick replaced James Shaw as a co-leader of the Green Party.

03-11.title: Hōne Heke's attack on Kororāreka
03-11.text: Hōne Heke's forces cut down the flagstaff at Kororāreka (Russell) for the fourth time and attacked the town, starting the Northern War.

03-11.title: Bridges names his first shadow cabinet
03-11.text: New National leader Simon Bridges announced his opposition line-up, with Gerry Brownlee as shadow leader of the House.

03-11.title: Electoral Amendment Act 2020 takes effect
03-11.text: Changes to electoral law came into force, including allowing voters to enrol on election day.

03-12.title: Joseph Ward resigns as prime minister
03-12.text: Liberal prime minister Sir Joseph Ward resigned after a disappointing election result. Thomas Mackenzie replaced him but lost office within months.

03-12.title: Bill on domestic violence and divorce passes
03-12.text: Parliament passed Labour MP Camilla Belich's member's bill as part of a run of opposition bills that became law in the 54th Parliament.

03-13.title: Marriage equality bill passes second reading
03-13.text: Louisa Wall's Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill passed its second reading. It became law the following month.

03-13.title: Voting-age change for general elections shelved
03-13.text: Prime Minister Chris Hipkins dropped plans to legislate for a voting age of 16 in general elections, focusing instead on local elections.

03-14.title: Capital moves to Auckland
03-14.text: Governor Hobson moved into his residence in Auckland, completing the shift of the capital from the Bay of Islands. Wellington took over as capital in 1865.

03-14.title: Self-isolation ordered for all arrivals
03-14.text: Jacinda Ardern announced that almost everyone entering New Zealand would have to self-isolate for 14 days, one of the world's strictest border rules at the time.

03-15.title: Christchurch mosque attacks
03-15.text: A terrorist killed 51 people at two Christchurch mosques. Within weeks Parliament banned most semi-automatic firearms, and the Government launched the Christchurch Call against online extremism.

03-15.title: Green MP Darleen Tana stood down
03-15.text: The Green Party stood down list MP Darleen Tana while allegations of migrant exploitation at her husband's business were investigated. She was later expelled.

03-16.title: Westland returns its first MP
03-16.text: William Moorhouse was returned for the new Westland seat during the 1866 general election.

03-16.title: Matiu Rata wins Northern Maori
03-16.text: Matiu Rata won the Northern Maori by-election for Labour. He later became Minister of Māori Affairs and set up the Waitangi Tribunal before founding Mana Motuhake.

03-16.title: Safe areas around abortion clinics
03-16.text: Parliament passed Louisa Wall's Safe Areas Amendment Act, 108 votes to 12, allowing protest-free zones of up to 150 metres around abortion providers.

03-17.title: First Taranaki War begins
03-17.text: Fighting broke out at Waitara over a disputed land sale, beginning the New Zealand Wars of the 1860s between the Crown and Māori.

03-17.title: Port Chalmers elects an MP
03-17.text: Thomas Dick was elected MP for Port Chalmers during the drawn-out 1866 general election.

03-18.title: Winston Peters quits National and his seat
03-18.text: Winston Peters resigned from the National Party and from Parliament, forcing a Tauranga by-election that he won as an independent before founding New Zealand First.

03-18.title: Abortion decriminalised
03-18.text: Parliament passed the Abortion Legislation Act, removing abortion from the Crimes Act and treating it as a health matter.

03-19.title: Bledisloe becomes Governor-General
03-19.text: Lord Bledisloe was sworn in as Governor-General. He later bought and gifted the Treaty House at Waitangi to the nation.

03-19.title: Borders closed to non-residents
03-19.text: The Government closed New Zealand's borders to almost everyone except citizens and residents because of COVID-19.

03-20.title: Māori chiefs choose a national flag
03-20.text: Northern chiefs meeting at James Busby's residence at Waitangi chose the flag of the United Tribes, New Zealand's first national flag.

03-20.title: Ngāti Whātua chief signs the Treaty
03-20.text: Apihai Te Kawau of Ngāti Whātua signed the Treaty of Waitangi at the Manukau Harbour. He later offered land for the new capital at Auckland.

03-20.title: Ban on semi-automatic firearms announced
03-20.text: Five days after the Christchurch mosque attacks, Jacinda Ardern announced that military-style semi-automatic weapons would be banned.

03-21.title: Hardie Boys becomes Governor-General
03-21.text: Sir Michael Hardie Boys succeeded Dame Catherine Tizard as Governor-General, months before the first MMP election.

03-21.title: Four-level alert system announced
03-21.text: Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced a four-level COVID-19 alert system. Four days later the whole country moved to level 4.

03-22.title: Jonathan Coleman resigns from Parliament
03-22.text: National's Jonathan Coleman resigned as MP for Northcote, triggering a by-election won by Dan Bidois.

03-23.title: Birth of Michael Joseph Savage
03-23.text: Michael Joseph Savage, who led the first Labour government from 1935 and introduced the welfare state, was born in Australia.

03-23.title: Abortion Legislation Act becomes law
03-23.text: The Abortion Legislation Act received royal assent. On the same day schools closed as New Zealand prepared for a national lockdown.

03-24.title: Te Whiti orders surveyors off Parihaka land
03-24.text: Te Whiti o Rongomai told his followers to remove government surveyors from confiscated land near Parihaka, starting a campaign of peaceful resistance.

03-24.title: Marine and Coastal Area Act passed
03-24.text: Parliament passed the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, replacing the 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act. It let iwi seek customary title through the courts.

03-25.title: First Labour government's Parliament opens
03-25.text: The 25th Parliament opened with Labour in government for the first time, under Michael Joseph Savage.

03-25.title: New Zealand enters level 4 lockdown
03-25.text: The country moved to alert level 4 at 11.59pm, closing most businesses and telling people to stay home. A state of national emergency was declared the same day.

03-26.title: Bolger replaces McLay as National leader
03-26.text: National MPs replaced Jim McLay with Jim Bolger as leader. Bolger became prime minister in 1990.

03-27.title: Death of Michael Joseph Savage
03-27.text: Prime Minister Michael Joseph Savage died in office. Peter Fraser succeeded him and led New Zealand through the Second World War.

03-28.title: CER trade agreement signed
03-28.text: Australia and New Zealand signed the Closer Economic Relations agreement, which removed most barriers to trade between the two countries.

03-28.title: Northland by-election
03-28.text: Winston Peters won the Northland by-election, taking a seat National had held for decades and reducing the Key government's majority.

03-28.title: Stuart Nash sacked from Cabinet
03-28.text: Prime Minister Chris Hipkins removed Stuart Nash from all ministerial roles after it emerged he had shared confidential Cabinet information with donors.

03-29.title: Christian Coalition announced
03-29.text: The Christian Heritage and Christian Democrat parties agreed to contest the first MMP election as the Christian Coalition. It fell just short of the 5 percent threshold.

03-29.title: Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority created
03-29.text: Prime Minister John Key announced CERA, a government agency with special powers to lead the rebuild of Christchurch after the February earthquake.

03-29.title: Louisa Wall announces resignation
03-29.text: Labour MP Louisa Wall, who sponsored the marriage equality law, announced she would leave Parliament.

03-30.title: Battle of Ōrākau
03-30.text: British forces surrounded Rewi Maniapoto's followers at Ōrākau in the Waikato. The battle, which ended on 2 April, was the last major engagement of the Waikato war.

03-30.title: Jonathan Hunt leaves Parliament
03-30.text: Former Speaker Jonathan Hunt left Parliament to become High Commissioner to the United Kingdom.

03-31.title: Māori Electoral Option Act takes effect
03-31.text: A new law let people of Māori descent switch between the Māori and general electoral rolls at almost any time, instead of only every few years.

04-01.title: Peter Fraser forms his first ministry
04-01.text: Peter Fraser formally became prime minister, five days after Michael Joseph Savage's death. He led Labour until 1949.

04-01.title: ACC scheme begins
04-01.text: The Accident Compensation scheme started, giving no-fault cover for injuries in return for giving up the right to sue.

04-01.title: Gun law changes introduced
04-01.text: The bill to ban most semi-automatic firearms was introduced to Parliament, 17 days after the Christchurch mosque attacks. It passed on 10 April.

04-02.title: Police raid on Maungapōhatu
04-02.text: About 70 armed police raided the Tūhoe prophet Rua Kēnana's community at Maungapōhatu to arrest him. Two Māori were killed, and the Supreme Court later found the arrest itself was illegal.

04-02.title: Savage announces the social security plan
04-02.text: Prime Minister Michael Joseph Savage used a national radio broadcast to set out Labour's plan for a comprehensive social security scheme, passed into law that September.

04-03.title: Anderton splits from the Alliance
04-03.text: Jim Anderton and Sandra Lee announced they would leave the Alliance, the party Anderton had founded, after a rift with its president. He formed the Progressive Coalition for the 2002 election.

04-03.title: Section 7AA repealed
04-03.text: Parliament passed the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Act, removing the child-welfare agency's Treaty obligations clause. The change was an ACT coalition commitment.

04-04.title: Silvia Cartwright becomes Governor-General
04-04.text: Dame Silvia Cartwright, a former High Court judge, was sworn in as the second woman to be Governor-General.

04-04.title: Committee reports on Treaty Principles Bill
04-04.text: The Justice select committee reported back on the Treaty Principles Bill, recommending it not proceed, after receiving a record number of public submissions.

04-05.title: Darren Hughes leaves Parliament
04-05.text: Labour MP Darren Hughes's resignation took effect after a police complaint against him, which did not result in charges.

04-05.title: Death of Sir Peter Tapsell
04-05.text: Sir Peter Tapsell, Speaker of the House from 1993 to 1996 and the first Māori to hold the office, died.

04-06.title: General election of 1866 ends
04-06.text: Polling in the 1866 general election, spread over nearly two months, came to an end. Māori electorates were created the following year.

04-06.title: George Grey returns to Parliament unopposed
04-06.text: Former governor and premier Sir George Grey was declared elected unopposed for an Auckland seat, in his last term in Parliament.

04-07.title: Free trade deal with China signed
04-07.text: New Zealand became the first developed country to sign a free trade agreement with China. Helen Clark attended the signing in Beijing.

04-08.title: Julius Vogel becomes premier
04-08.text: Julius Vogel formed his first ministry. He is remembered for borrowing heavily to build railways and bring in immigrants.

04-08.title: National and Greens sign memorandum
04-08.text: The National-led government and the Green Party signed a memorandum of understanding to work together on home insulation and other areas.

04-08.title: Marama Davidson elected Green co-leader
04-08.text: Marama Davidson won the Green Party's female co-leadership, replacing Metiria Turei who had resigned after the 2017 election.

04-09.title: Historical homosexual convictions can be wiped
04-09.text: A law allowing men convicted under old anti-homosexuality laws to have their convictions expunged received royal assent.

04-10.title: Special referendum on prohibition
04-10.text: A nationwide vote on banning alcohol narrowly failed after the votes of soldiers returning from the war were counted.

04-10.title: Semi-automatic firearms banned
04-10.text: Parliament passed the Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 119 votes to 1, less than a month after the Christchurch attacks.

04-10.title: Treaty Principles Bill voted down
04-10.text: Parliament defeated ACT's Treaty Principles Bill at its second reading, 112 votes to 11. Only ACT voted for it.

04-11.title: Gun law receives royal assent
04-11.text: The firearms ban became law when the Governor-General signed the Arms Amendment Act.

04-12.title: Galway becomes Governor-General
04-12.text: Viscount Galway was sworn in as Governor-General, months before Labour's first election win.

04-12.title: Māori Party referred to police over donations
04-12.text: The Electoral Commission referred Te Pāti Māori to police over late declaration of 2020 election donations.

04-13.title: Three Waters reforms reworked
04-13.text: The Government renamed its Three Waters programme the Water Services Reform Programme and increased the planned number of water entities from four to ten.

04-14.title: Birth of George Grey
04-14.text: George Grey, twice Governor of New Zealand and later premier, was born in Lisbon.

04-15.title: Second Parliament opens
04-15.text: The 2nd Parliament opened in Auckland. Within weeks it won the right to responsible government, with ministers answerable to the House.

04-15.title: Tamihere and Ngarewa-Packer take Māori Party roles
04-15.text: The Māori Party announced John Tamihere as president and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer as a co-leader as it rebuilt for the 2020 election.

04-16.title: Omata by-election
04-16.text: James Crowe Richmond was returned unopposed for Omata in Taranaki, during the war then being fought in the province.

04-17.title: Peters wins Tauranga by-election as an independent
04-17.text: Winston Peters won back his Tauranga seat as an independent with more than 90 percent of the vote. Three months later he launched New Zealand First.

04-17.title: Same-sex marriage legalised
04-17.text: Parliament passed Louisa Wall's Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill 77 votes to 44, making New Zealand the first country in the Asia-Pacific to legalise same-sex marriage.

04-17.title: New electorate boundaries set
04-17.text: The Representation Commission released final electorate boundaries for the 2014 election, adding a seat in Auckland.

04-18.title: Pay equity settlement for care workers
04-18.text: The Government announced a $2 billion pay equity settlement for care and support workers, following Kristine Bartlett's court case.

04-19.title: Newall ends term as Governor-General
04-19.text: Sir Cyril Newall's wartime term as Governor-General ended. Lord Freyberg succeeded him in June.

04-19.title: Marriage equality law receives royal assent
04-19.text: The Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Act received royal assent. The first same-sex weddings took place in August 2013.

04-20.title: Taito Phillip Field goes on trial
04-20.text: The trial of former Labour MP Taito Phillip Field on bribery and corruption charges began in the Auckland High Court. He was found guilty in August.

04-20.title: Police watchdog reports on Parliament protest
04-20.text: The Independent Police Conduct Authority released its report on policing of the 2022 occupation of Parliament grounds, finding most officers acted with restraint.

04-21.title: Hall ministry ends
04-21.text: John Hall's ministry, which had passed the Triennial Parliaments Act and votes for all adult men, gave way to Frederick Whitaker's government.

04-22.title: Rātana and Labour form an alliance
04-22.text: T. W. Rātana met Prime Minister Michael Joseph Savage and the Rātana movement agreed to work with Labour. The alliance helped Labour hold the Māori seats for decades.

04-23.title: Review of local government announced
04-23.text: Local Government Minister Nanaia Mahuta announced an independent review of the future of local government.

04-23.title: Cyclone Gabrielle inquiry reports
04-23.text: The Government released the final report of the inquiry into the response to Cyclone Gabrielle and the 2023 Auckland floods.

04-24.title: Cabinet reshuffle drops Melissa Lee
04-24.text: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon removed Melissa Lee from Cabinet and the media portfolio, and Penny Simmonds from the disability portfolio.

04-25.title: First Anzac Day
04-25.text: The first Anzac Day commemorations were held one year after the Gallipoli landings. Anzac Day became a public holiday under a 1920 Act.

04-26.title: Don Brash leaves the Reserve Bank for politics
04-26.text: Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash resigned to stand for National at the 2002 election. He became National's leader in 2003.

04-26.title: Civil unions begin
04-26.text: The Civil Union Act 2004 took effect, allowing same-sex and opposite-sex couples to register civil unions.

04-27.title: Premier John Ballance dies
04-27.text: Liberal premier John Ballance died in office. Richard Seddon succeeded him and governed for 13 years.

04-28.title: Cave Creek platform collapse
04-28.text: A Department of Conservation viewing platform collapsed at Cave Creek, killing 14 people. A commission of inquiry found systemic failures, and the Minister of Conservation later resigned.

04-28.title: Rodney Hide resigns as ACT leader
04-28.text: Rodney Hide stepped down as ACT leader and was replaced by former National leader Don Brash.

04-29.title: Parekura Horomia dies
04-29.text: Labour's Parekura Horomia, MP for Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and former Minister of Māori Affairs, died. Meka Whaitiri won the by-election in June.

04-30.title: Tariana Turia quits Labour
04-30.text: Minister Tariana Turia announced she was leaving the Labour Party over the foreshore and seabed legislation. She co-founded the Māori Party weeks later.

04-30.title: Mana Party launched
04-30.text: Hone Harawira formally launched the Mana Party after leaving the Māori Party.

05-01.title: Richard Seddon becomes premier
05-01.text: Richard Seddon took over as Liberal premier after John Ballance's death. 'King Dick' held office until his own death in 1906, the longest tenure of any New Zealand leader.

05-01.title: NewLabour Party launched
05-01.text: Jim Anderton left Labour in protest at its economic policies and launched the NewLabour Party, a forerunner of the Alliance.

05-02.title: Taranaki-King Country by-election
05-02.text: National's Shane Ardern held the Taranaki-King Country seat after Jim Bolger left Parliament, in a by-election marked by a strong ACT showing.

05-03.title: New Zealand becomes a separate colony
05-03.text: New Zealand ceased to be part of New South Wales and became a Crown colony in its own right, with its own Governor and appointed Legislative Council.

05-03.title: Meka Whaitiri defects to Te Pāti Māori
05-03.text: Minister Meka Whaitiri announced she was leaving Labour for Te Pāti Māori, the first sitting minister to switch parties in decades.

05-04.title: 'Three strikes' bill passes second reading
05-04.text: The Sentencing and Parole Reform Bill passed its second reading 63 votes to 59, with National and ACT in favour.

05-04.title: Harawira delays his resignation
05-04.text: Hone Harawira put off resigning his seat to consult supporters, after criticism of his plan to force a by-election. He resigned a week later.

05-05.title: Foreshore and seabed hīkoi reaches Parliament
05-05.text: A hīkoi (march) of around 15,000 people arrived at Parliament to oppose the Foreshore and Seabed Bill, which was passed later that year.

05-05.title: Mana Movement deregistered
05-05.text: The Mana Movement, founded by Hone Harawira in 2011, had its registration cancelled at its own request.

05-06.title: James Shaw leaves Parliament
05-06.text: Former Green co-leader and Climate Change Minister James Shaw resigned from Parliament.

05-07.title: First responsible government
05-07.text: Henry Sewell formed New Zealand's first ministry answerable to the elected House, though it lasted only two weeks.

05-07.title: Pay equity law changed under urgency
05-07.text: Parliament passed the Equal Pay Amendment Act under urgency, raising the bar for pay equity claims and halting claims already under way.

05-08.title: Zero Carbon Bill introduced
05-08.text: The Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill was introduced, setting a target of net zero emissions by 2050. It passed in November with near-unanimous support.

05-09.title: Graeme Lee leaves National
05-09.text: National MP Graeme Lee quit the party to form the Christian Democrat Party, one of several defections before the first MMP election.

05-09.title: Treaty Principles claim lodged
05-09.text: Ngāpuhi kaumātua Hone Sadler and others lodged an urgent Waitangi Tribunal claim against the Government's Treaty Principles Bill.

05-10.title: Death of William Massey
05-10.text: Prime Minister William Massey died in office after nearly 13 years leading the Reform government.

05-11.title: Harawira resigns to force a by-election
05-11.text: Hone Harawira resigned his Te Tai Tokerau seat to seek a fresh mandate under his new Mana Party banner. He won the by-election in June.

05-12.title: COVID-19 Public Health Response Bill
05-12.text: Parliament debated the COVID-19 Public Health Response Bill, which gave the Government legal powers for alert-level orders. It passed the next day with National opposed.

05-13.title: Internet Party registered
05-13.text: The Electoral Commission registered the Internet Party, funded by Kim Dotcom. It later joined with Mana to contest the 2014 election.

05-14.title: Francis Bell becomes prime minister
05-14.text: Sir Francis Bell took over as prime minister after Massey's death. He served only 16 days and remains the shortest-serving prime minister.

05-14.title: National Party founded
05-14.text: The New Zealand National Party was formed at a meeting in Wellington on 13 and 14 May 1936, bringing together the United and Reform parties after Labour's 1935 win.

05-14.title: Record suspensions proposed over haka
05-14.text: The Privileges Committee recommended suspending three Te Pāti Māori MPs for performing a haka during the Treaty Principles Bill vote, the longest suspensions ever proposed.

05-15.title: Christchurch Call launched
05-15.text: Jacinda Ardern and French President Emmanuel Macron launched the Christchurch Call in Paris, asking governments and tech companies to curb terrorist content online.

05-16.title: 'Anti-smacking' law passes
05-16.text: Parliament passed Sue Bradford's bill removing the defence of reasonable force for parents who hit children, by 113 votes to 8 after a compromise brokered by John Key and Helen Clark.

05-17.title: Turia resigns from Parliament
05-17.text: Tariana Turia resigned her Te Tai Hauāuru seat and won it back in a by-election in July as the Māori Party's first MP.

05-18.title: Eighth Parliament opens
05-18.text: The 8th Parliament opened after the 1881 election, the first held under the new law giving the vote to all adult men.

05-19.title: Voters reject Māori wards in five districts
05-19.text: Binding local polls in Palmerston North, Western Bay of Plenty, Whakatāne, Manawatū and Kaikōura overturned council decisions to create Māori wards.

05-20.title: Fox's first ministry
05-20.text: William Fox formed a ministry that lasted just 13 days before Edward Stafford took over.

05-20.title: Māori wards poll bill introduced
05-20.text: The Government introduced legislation requiring councils that had set up Māori wards without a poll to hold one or scrap the wards.

05-21.title: Hobson proclaims British sovereignty
05-21.text: Lieutenant-Governor Hobson proclaimed British sovereignty over all of New Zealand: the North Island by treaty and the South Island by discovery.

05-21.title: Pike River mine re-entry begins
05-21.text: A recovery team re-entered the Pike River mine drift for the first time since the 2010 explosions, fulfilling a promise by the Labour-led government.

05-22.title: Waikato-Tainui settlement signed
05-22.text: The Crown and Waikato-Tainui signed a deed settling raupatu (land confiscation) claims, worth $170 million. It was the first major Treaty settlement.

05-22.title: Todd Muller replaces Simon Bridges
05-22.text: National MPs replaced Simon Bridges with Todd Muller as leader after poor polls during the COVID-19 lockdown. Muller resigned 53 days later.

05-23.title: Hobson rules Wellington settlers' council illegal
05-23.text: Hobson declared that the New Zealand Company settlers' self-appointed council at Port Nicholson had no legal authority.

05-24.title: First Parliament meets
05-24.text: New Zealand's first General Assembly met in Auckland. Members had been elected in 1853 under the Constitution Act 1852.

05-24.title: Phil Twyford gives up aviation role
05-24.text: Transport Minister Phil Twyford resigned as Minister of Civil Aviation after making a phone call on a plane after the doors had closed.

05-24.title: Royal commission into mosque attacks
05-24.text: Cabinet announced the terms of a royal commission of inquiry into the Christchurch mosque attacks. It reported in November 2020.

05-25.title: Bastion Point occupiers removed
05-25.text: About 800 police and army personnel ended the 506-day occupation of Bastion Point, arresting 222 people. The land was later returned to Ngāti Whātua.

05-25.title: 'Three strikes' law passed
05-25.text: Parliament passed the Sentencing and Parole Reform Act, introducing a three-strikes regime for serious violent offences. It was repealed in 2022 and reinstated in 2024.

05-26.title: Parihaka ploughmen begin
05-26.text: Followers of Te Whiti began ploughing settlers' land in Taranaki as a peaceful protest against confiscation. Hundreds were arrested and held without trial.

05-26.title: Alliance deregistered
05-26.text: The Alliance, which had been part of the 1999 government, had its registration cancelled at its own request.

05-27.title: MP killed in the Waikato war
05-27.text: Marmaduke Nixon, MP for Franklin, died of wounds received during the invasion of Waikato.

05-28.title: Forbes replaces Ward as prime minister
05-28.text: George Forbes took over as United Party prime minister from the ailing Sir Joseph Ward as the Depression deepened.

05-28.title: Anti-apartheid protest in Christchurch
05-28.text: A protest against sporting contact with South Africa was held in Cathedral Square, part of a movement that peaked during the 1981 Springbok tour.

05-28.title: Green Party founded
05-28.text: The Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand was founded at a conference in late May 1990, growing out of the Values Party and environmental groups.

05-29.title: Grey by-election after an MP is jailed
05-29.text: A by-election was held in Grey after Labour MP Paddy Webb was imprisoned for opposing conscription. Labour's Harry Holland won the seat.

05-29.title: Laila Harré leads the Internet Party
05-29.text: Former Alliance minister Laila Harré was named the first leader of the Internet Party.

05-30.title: Gordon Coates becomes prime minister
05-30.text: The Reform Party chose Gordon Coates as prime minister after Francis Bell's brief caretaker term.

05-30.title: Values Party founded
05-30.text: The Values Party, often described as the world's first national environmental party, was launched in Wellington.

05-30.title: First Wellbeing Budget
05-30.text: Grant Robertson delivered the Government's first 'Wellbeing Budget', which set spending priorities around wellbeing measures as well as GDP.

05-31.title: United Future loses registration
05-31.text: The Electoral Commission cancelled United Future's registration after the party could not show it had 500 members. It was re-registered in August.

05-31.title: Seymour becomes deputy prime minister
05-31.text: ACT leader David Seymour took over as deputy prime minister from Winston Peters, under the coalition agreement that split the role between them.

06-01.title: Destiny New Zealand registered
06-01.text: The Electoral Commission registered Destiny New Zealand, the party linked to Destiny Church. It won 0.6 percent in 2005.

06-01.title: 'Three strikes' regime takes effect
06-01.text: The three-strikes sentencing law began applying to serious offences committed from this day.

06-02.title: Stafford forms the first stable ministry
06-02.text: Edward Stafford became premier, leading New Zealand's first lasting government under responsible rule. His ministry survived until 1861.

06-03.title: Third Parliament opens
06-03.text: The 3rd Parliament opened in Auckland as war in Taranaki and the Waikato dominated politics.

06-03.title: Richard Worth resigns as minister
06-03.text: Internal Affairs Minister Richard Worth resigned after allegations about his conduct. He later left Parliament.

06-04.title: Death of Walter Nash
06-04.text: Sir Walter Nash, prime minister from 1957 to 1960, died aged 86 while still an MP, triggering a by-election in Hutt.

06-04.title: ACT launches 2023 campaign
06-04.text: ACT launched its election campaign, promising a Ministry of Regulation and a new law on regulatory standards.

06-05.title: Three MPs suspended over haka
06-05.text: Parliament voted along party lines to suspend Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke for seven days and Te Pāti Māori co-leaders Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer for 21 days.

06-06.title: Lord Glasgow becomes Governor
06-06.text: The Earl of Glasgow took office as Governor. In 1893 he signed the Electoral Act giving women the vote.

06-07.title: Death of Elizabeth McCombs
06-07.text: Elizabeth McCombs, New Zealand's first woman MP, died less than two years after winning the Lyttelton by-election.

06-07.title: Pae Ora health reforms passed
06-07.text: Parliament passed the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act, replacing district health boards with Te Whatu Ora and creating the Māori Health Authority, Te Aka Whai Ora.

06-08.title: Nuclear-free law passed
06-08.text: Parliament passed the New Zealand Nuclear Free Zone, Disarmament, and Arms Control Act, banning nuclear-armed and nuclear-powered ships from New Zealand waters.

06-08.title: Jan Tinetti referred to Privileges Committee
06-08.text: Education Minister Jan Tinetti was referred to the Privileges Committee for not correcting a misleading answer about truancy data. She later apologised to the House.

06-09.title: Northcote by-election
06-09.text: National's Dan Bidois held the Northcote seat in a by-election after Jonathan Coleman's resignation.

06-10.title: Death of Richard Seddon
06-10.text: Premier Richard Seddon died at sea on his way home from Australia after 13 years in office.

06-10.title: Inquiry into Māori Party data allegations
06-10.text: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announced a Public Service Commission inquiry into allegations that census data was misused for Te Pāti Māori's 2023 campaign.

06-11.title: Cook Islands and Niue become part of New Zealand
06-11.text: The Cook Islands and Niue were annexed to the Colony of New Zealand. Both are now self-governing in free association with New Zealand.

06-12.title: Internet Party deregistered
06-12.text: The Internet Party was deregistered after its membership fell below 500.

06-13.title: Mount Albert by-election
06-13.text: David Shearer won the Mount Albert by-election for Labour after Helen Clark left Parliament to head the UN Development Programme.

06-14.title: FitzGerald's short-lived ministry
06-14.text: James FitzGerald led a four-person ministry, New Zealand's first attempt at a government answerable to Parliament. It fell within weeks when the Governor refused full responsible government.

06-14.title: Muldoon calls a snap election
06-14.text: Prime Minister Robert Muldoon announced a snap election for 14 July after National MP Marilyn Waring said she would back an opposition nuclear-free bill. Labour won in a landslide.

06-15.title: New Zealand brought within New South Wales
06-15.text: New letters patent extended the boundaries of New South Wales to include New Zealand, preparing the way for Hobson's mission.

06-15.title: Sixth Parliament opens
06-15.text: The 6th Parliament opened in Wellington. Later that year it abolished the provinces.

06-16.title: Labour becomes the official Opposition
06-16.text: Harry Holland became Leader of the Opposition after a by-election win gave Labour more seats than the Liberals.

06-17.title: Wairau Affray
06-17.text: Fighting at Wairau between Ngāti Toa and armed settlers from Nelson left 22 Europeans and at least four Māori dead. It was the first serious armed clash after the Treaty.

06-17.title: Freyberg becomes Governor-General
06-17.text: Lord Freyberg, who had commanded New Zealand's forces in the Second World War, was sworn in as Governor-General.

06-18.title: Tauranga by-election
06-18.text: National's Sam Uffindell won the Tauranga by-election after Simon Bridges left Parliament.

06-19.title: Colin Craig resigns as Conservative leader
06-19.text: Conservative Party founder Colin Craig stepped down as leader amid allegations about his conduct towards a former press secretary.

06-20.title: Peters becomes acting prime minister
06-20.text: Winston Peters took over as acting prime minister when Jacinda Ardern went into labour. He held the role for six weeks.

06-21.title: First use of the title 'Prime Minister'
06-21.text: William Hall-Jones was sworn in as head of government, the first to be given the title Prime Minister rather than Premier. He held the job for six weeks.

06-21.title: Michael Wood resigns from Cabinet
06-21.text: Michael Wood resigned as a minister after failing to declare shareholdings that conflicted with his portfolios.

06-22.title: Birth of Richard Seddon
06-22.text: Richard John Seddon, New Zealand's longest-serving leader, was born in Lancashire, England.

06-23.title: Petition for smacking referendum delivered
06-23.text: Kiwi Party leader Larry Baldock presented a petition seeking a citizens-initiated referendum on the 2007 'anti-smacking' law.

06-23.title: Death of Koro Wētere
06-23.text: Koro Wētere, Labour MP for Western Maori from 1969 to 1996 and Minister of Māori Affairs in the Lange government, died.

06-24.title: Parliament opens in wartime
06-24.text: The 19th Parliament opened. Within weeks Reform and the Liberals formed a wartime coalition government.

06-24.title: First Matariki public holiday
06-24.text: New Zealand marked Matariki, the Māori new year, as a public holiday for the first time, under legislation passed in April 2022.

06-25.title: Prostitution decriminalised
06-25.text: Parliament passed Tim Barnett's Prostitution Reform Bill by a single vote, 60 to 59, decriminalising sex work.

06-25.title: Te Tai Tokerau by-election
06-25.text: Hone Harawira won the Te Tai Tokerau by-election for the new Mana Party, defeating Labour's Kelvin Davis.

06-26.title: The 'Black Budget'
06-26.text: Finance Minister Arnold Nordmeyer raised taxes on beer, tobacco, cars and petrol in a Budget that became known as the Black Budget and hurt Labour at the 1960 election.

06-26.title: Death of Takutai Tarsh Kemp
06-26.text: Te Pāti Māori MP Takutai Tarsh Kemp, who had won Tāmaki Makaurau in 2023, died. A by-election followed in September.

06-27.title: Russel Norman enters Parliament
06-27.text: Green co-leader Russel Norman entered Parliament from the party list after Nándor Tánczos resigned.

06-27.title: Ardern reshuffles Cabinet
06-27.text: Jacinda Ardern announced a Cabinet reshuffle, including changes to the housing portfolio after the KiwiBuild programme fell short of its targets.

06-28.title: Governor becomes Governor-General
06-28.text: The title of New Zealand's vice-regal representative changed from Governor to Governor-General.

06-28.title: United New Zealand formed
06-28.text: Seven MPs from National and Labour, led by Clive Matthewson and including Peter Dunne, formed the centrist United New Zealand party.

06-29.title: The 'Lands case' judgment
06-29.text: The Court of Appeal ruled in New Zealand Maori Council v Attorney-General that the Crown must act consistently with Treaty principles when transferring assets to state enterprises. The ruling shaped Treaty law.

06-29.title: Ikaroa-Rāwhiti by-election
06-29.text: Labour's Meka Whaitiri won the Ikaroa-Rāwhiti by-election following the death of Parekura Horomia.

06-30.title: Constitution Act 1852 passed
06-30.text: The British Parliament passed the New Zealand Constitution Act, creating an elected House of Representatives, an appointed Legislative Council and six provinces.

06-30.title: War Administration formed
06-30.text: Labour and National formed a joint War Administration to run the war effort. It collapsed within months over a coal miners' strike.

07-01.title: Supreme Court sits for the first time
07-01.text: New Zealand's new Supreme Court heard its first case, six months after it replaced the Privy Council as the final court of appeal.

07-02.title: KiwiSaver begins
07-02.text: The KiwiSaver voluntary retirement savings scheme started operating, with employer and government contributions.

07-02.title: Wai 262 report released
07-02.text: The Waitangi Tribunal released Ko Aotearoa Tēnei, its report on the Wai 262 claim about Māori knowledge, culture and native plants and animals, after 20 years of hearings.

07-02.title: David Clark resigns as Health Minister
07-02.text: David Clark resigned as Minister of Health after breaching lockdown rules and clashing with health officials during the COVID-19 response.

07-03.title: Ron Mark becomes NZ First deputy leader
07-03.text: Ron Mark replaced Tracey Martin as deputy leader of New Zealand First.

07-04.title: Marshall warned of Muldoon challenge
07-04.text: Opposition leader Jack Marshall was told that his deputy Robert Muldoon was about to challenge him. Marshall stepped down days later.

07-04.title: Botany march on crime
07-04.text: Thousands of mostly Asian New Zealanders marched in Auckland against the Labour government's record on crime, in an election-year protest.

07-05.title: Mackenzie government loses confidence vote
07-05.text: Thomas Mackenzie's Liberal ministry was defeated on a no-confidence motion, 41 votes to 33, ending the Liberal era.

07-06.title: Pollen ministry takes office
07-06.text: Daniel Pollen became premier after Julius Vogel stepped aside. His ministry oversaw the law abolishing the provinces.

07-07.title: Labour Party founded
07-07.text: The New Zealand Labour Party was founded in Wellington, uniting several earlier socialist and union-based groups. It first won government in 1935.

07-07.title: Māori Party established
07-07.text: The Māori Party was formally established, led by Tariana Turia and Pita Sharples, after the foreshore and seabed dispute. It is now Te Pāti Māori.

07-08.title: Liverpool ends term as Governor-General
07-08.text: The Earl of Liverpool, the last Governor and first Governor-General of New Zealand, finished his term.

07-08.title: UN ruling on the Rainbow Warrior
07-08.text: UN Secretary-General Javier Pérez de Cuéllar ruled that France must apologise and pay New Zealand compensation for bombing the Rainbow Warrior, and that the two agents be held on a Pacific atoll.

07-09.title: Homosexual Law Reform Bill passes
07-09.text: Parliament passed Fran Wilde's Homosexual Law Reform Bill 49 votes to 44, decriminalising sex between men after a bitter public campaign.

07-09.title: Greens launch 2017 campaign
07-09.text: The Green Party launched its election campaign with a proposed levy on companies exporting bottled water.

07-10.title: Massey becomes prime minister
07-10.text: William Massey's Reform Party took office after the Liberal government lost a confidence vote, ending 21 years of Liberal rule.

07-10.title: Rainbow Warrior bombed
07-10.text: French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour, killing photographer Fernando Pereira. The attack strained relations with France for years.

07-10.title: Turia wins Te Tai Hauāuru for the Māori Party
07-10.text: Tariana Turia won back her seat in a by-election as the first Māori Party MP, after resigning from Labour over the foreshore and seabed law.

07-11.title: Homosexual Law Reform Act becomes law
07-11.text: The Homosexual Law Reform Act received royal assent two days after passing Parliament.

07-12.title: Fox replaces Stafford as premier
07-12.text: William Fox formed his second ministry after Edward Stafford's five-year government fell over the handling of the Taranaki war.

07-12.title: Invasion of the Waikato begins
07-12.text: British troops crossed the Mangatāwhiri Stream into Waikato, beginning the largest campaign of the New Zealand Wars. Large areas of land were later confiscated.

07-12.title: Te Pāti Māori name registered
07-12.text: The Māori Party formally registered its new name, Te Pāti Māori, with the Electoral Commission.

07-13.title: Death of Kate Sheppard
07-13.text: Kate Sheppard, leader of the women's suffrage campaign, died in Christchurch aged 86.

07-13.title: Deadline to switch rolls for the 2023 election
07-13.text: The cut-off passed for people of Māori descent to switch between the Māori and general rolls before the 2023 election, under new rules allowing changes at most times.

07-14.title: Bill to hold Parihaka prisoners without trial
07-14.text: Native Minister John Bryce introduced a bill allowing Māori arrested for ploughing at Parihaka to be held without trial.

07-14.title: Labour wins the snap election
07-14.text: David Lange's Labour Party won a landslide in the snap election called by Robert Muldoon. The result was followed by a currency crisis and far-reaching economic reforms.

07-14.title: Judith Collins becomes National leader
07-14.text: Todd Muller resigned after 53 days as National leader and the caucus chose Judith Collins to lead the party into the 2020 election.

07-15.title: Waterfront dispute ends
07-15.text: The 151-day waterfront dispute ended in defeat for the watersiders' union. Sidney Holland called a snap election soon after and increased his majority.

07-16.title: War Cabinet formed
07-16.text: Labour and National formed a joint War Cabinet to direct New Zealand's part in the Second World War.

07-17.title: Parliament TV goes on air
07-17.text: Live television coverage of Parliament began, adding to the radio broadcasts that had run since the 1930s.

07-17.title: Death of Sir Bill Birch
07-17.text: Sir William Birch, Minister of Finance from 1993 to 1999 and a minister under three prime ministers, died aged 92.

07-18.title: New Zealand First founded
07-18.text: Winston Peters launched New Zealand First in Auckland, shortly before the 1993 election. The party has held the balance of power several times since.

07-19.title: Springboks arrive
07-19.text: The South African rugby team arrived for a 56-day tour that split the country and brought the largest protests since the 1951 waterfront dispute.

07-19.title: Peters promises referendum on Māori seats
07-19.text: Winston Peters said a New Zealand First government would hold a referendum on abolishing the Māori electorates.

07-20.title: Birth of Pita Sharples
07-20.text: Sir Pita Sharples, co-founder and co-leader of the Māori Party from 2004 to 2013, was born.

07-20.title: Death of Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan
07-20.text: Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan, who held Southern Maori for 29 years and was the first Māori woman Cabinet minister, died.

07-21.title: Andrew Falloon resigns
07-21.text: National MP Andrew Falloon resigned from Parliament after it was revealed he had sent explicit images to young women.

07-22.title: General election of 1884
07-22.text: Voters in the general electorates went to the polls, a day after the Māori electorates. The result led to Robert Stout and Julius Vogel forming a government.

07-22.title: Iain Lees-Galloway sacked
07-22.text: Jacinda Ardern dismissed Workplace Relations Minister Iain Lees-Galloway over an inappropriate relationship with a former staff member.

07-23.title: Birth of Te Atairangikaahu
07-23.text: Dame Te Atairangikaahu, Māori Queen from 1966 to 2006 and head of the Kīngitanga, was born.

07-23.title: Electoral Finance Bill introduced
07-23.text: Justice Minister Mark Burton introduced the Electoral Finance Bill, which tightened rules on third-party campaigning and became one of the most contested laws of the Clark government.

07-24.title: Internet Mana registered
07-24.text: The Electoral Commission registered the Internet Mana alliance, letting the Internet Party and Mana contest the party vote together.

07-24.title: Kiri Allan resigns from Cabinet
07-24.text: Justice Minister Kiri Allan resigned after being arrested following a car crash in Wellington.

07-24.title: Abuse in Care inquiry reports
07-24.text: The Royal Commission into Abuse in Care delivered its final report, finding about 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care. The Government apologised in November.

07-25.title: Hamilton Springbok match cancelled
07-25.text: Protesters invaded Rugby Park in Hamilton and the Springboks' match against Waikato was called off, a turning point in the 1981 tour.

07-26.title: Parliament meets in Wellington for the first time
07-26.text: Parliament opened its session in Wellington, which had replaced Auckland as the capital.

07-26.title: Fourth Labour Government takes office
07-26.text: David Lange was sworn in as prime minister after the snap election. His government began sweeping economic reforms known as Rogernomics.

07-27.title: General election of 2002
07-27.text: Helen Clark's Labour Party was re-elected. National fell to 20.9 percent, its worst result, while New Zealand First and United Future gained.

07-28.title: Suffrage petition presented to Parliament
07-28.text: Sir John Hall presented the women's suffrage petition, signed by nearly 32,000 women, unrolling it along the floor of the House.

07-28.title: Pahiatua MP dies
07-28.text: James Escott, Reform MP for Pahiatua, died, leading to a wartime by-election.

07-28.title: Extradition treaty with Hong Kong suspended
07-28.text: Foreign Minister Winston Peters announced New Zealand was suspending its extradition treaty with Hong Kong in response to China's national security law.

07-29.title: NZ Loyal deregistered
07-29.text: NZ Loyal, the party founded by Liz Gunn for the 2023 election, had its registration cancelled at its own request.

07-29.title: Electoral Amendment Bill passes first reading
07-29.text: The Government's Electoral Amendment Bill, which ended same-day enrolment and made other changes before the 2026 election, passed its first reading along party lines.

07-30.title: Māori ward polls reinstated
07-30.text: A law requiring councils to hold binding polls on Māori wards, or scrap them, came into force. Polls were held alongside the 2025 local elections.

07-31.title: Referendum on 'smacking' begins
07-31.text: Postal voting opened in a citizens-initiated referendum asking whether a smack as part of parental correction should be a criminal offence. Voting closed on 21 August.

07-31.title: Te Pāti Māori goes to court over Māori roll
07-31.text: Te Pāti Māori filed urgent High Court proceedings over reports that voters had been moved off the Māori roll without consent.

08-01.title: Te reo Māori becomes an official language
08-01.text: The Māori Language Act 1987 came into force, making te reo Māori an official language and creating the Māori Language Commission.

08-01.title: Jacinda Ardern becomes Labour leader
08-01.text: Andrew Little stepped down seven weeks before the election and Jacinda Ardern was elected Labour leader unopposed.

08-01.title: Apology for the Dawn Raids
08-01.text: Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern formally apologised to Pacific communities for the Dawn Raids of the 1970s, when police targeted alleged overstayers.

08-02.title: Lyttelton MP James McCombs dies
08-02.text: Labour's James McCombs died. His widow Elizabeth won the by-election and became New Zealand's first woman MP.

08-02.title: Ardern returns from maternity leave
08-02.text: Jacinda Ardern resumed duties as prime minister after six weeks' leave, during which Winston Peters was acting prime minister.

08-03.title: Referendum on compulsory military training
08-03.text: Voters backed peacetime compulsory military training in a referendum called by the Fraser government.

08-03.title: Caucus brings back Roger Douglas
08-03.text: The Labour caucus voted to return Roger Douglas to Cabinet. David Lange treated the vote as a loss of confidence and resigned days later.

08-03.title: Conservative Party founded
08-03.text: Businessman Colin Craig announced the formation of the Conservative Party in Auckland.

08-04.title: Birth of David Lange
08-04.text: David Lange, prime minister from 1984 to 1989 and the voice of New Zealand's nuclear-free policy, was born in Otahuhu.

08-04.title: Cook Islands self-government
08-04.text: The Cook Islands' constitution came into force, making the islands self-governing in free association with New Zealand.

08-04.title: Taito Phillip Field found guilty
08-04.text: Former Labour MP Taito Phillip Field was found guilty of bribery and corruption charges, the first MP convicted of such offences.

08-05.title: Death of Robert Muldoon
08-05.text: Sir Robert Muldoon, prime minister from 1975 to 1984, died aged 70.

08-05.title: Abortion law reform announced
08-05.text: Justice Minister Andrew Little announced legislation to take abortion out of the Crimes Act. The law passed in March 2020.

08-06.title: Alfred Domett becomes premier
08-06.text: Poet and politician Alfred Domett replaced William Fox as premier.

08-06.title: Joseph Ward becomes prime minister
08-06.text: Sir Joseph Ward took over the Liberal government after William Hall-Jones's brief caretaker term following Richard Seddon's death.

08-06.title: Parliament's last scheduled sitting before the election
08-06.text: The 52nd Parliament held what was meant to be its final sitting day. A COVID-19 outbreak days later delayed its dissolution and the election.

08-07.title: Ninth Parliament opens
08-07.text: The 9th Parliament opened after the 1884 election. It saw four different ministries in three years.

08-07.title: David Lange announces his resignation
08-07.text: David Lange announced he was resigning as prime minister after his caucus restored Roger Douglas to Cabinet.

08-08.title: Geoffrey Palmer becomes prime minister
08-08.text: Geoffrey Palmer was sworn in as prime minister after David Lange's resignation. He resigned himself 13 months later.

08-09.title: Metiria Turei resigns as Green co-leader
08-09.text: Metiria Turei stepped down as Green co-leader after admitting she had misled Work and Income while a student, a disclosure that shook the party's campaign.

08-09.title: 'Three strikes' law repealed
08-09.text: Parliament passed the Three Strikes Legislation Repeal Act. The regime was reinstated in a different form in 2024.

08-10.title: Human Rights Act 1993
08-10.text: The Human Rights Act, which brought together anti-discrimination law and added new grounds such as sexual orientation and disability, received royal assent.

08-11.title: Parliament dissolved for the 2005 election
08-11.text: The 47th Parliament ended, leading to a close election between Helen Clark's Labour and Don Brash's National.

08-11.title: Auckland returns to lockdown
08-11.text: After the first community COVID-19 cases in 102 days, the Government put Auckland back into alert level 3 and the rest of the country into level 2.

08-12.title: Dissolution of Parliament delayed
08-12.text: Jacinda Ardern delayed the dissolution of Parliament after new COVID-19 cases in Auckland. The election was later moved from September to October.

08-13.title: Electoral Commission proposes MMP changes
08-13.text: The Electoral Commission proposed lowering the party-vote threshold to 4 percent and scrapping the one-seat rule. The National government did not adopt the changes.

08-13.title: United Future re-registered
08-13.text: The Electoral Commission accepted United Future's application to be re-registered after it had lost registration in May.

08-14.title: Fifth Parliament opens
08-14.text: The 5th Parliament opened. Its term saw six different ministries and Julius Vogel's borrowing programme.

08-14.title: Shipley sacks Peters; coalition collapses
08-14.text: Prime Minister Jenny Shipley dismissed Winston Peters from Cabinet, ending the National-New Zealand First coalition. National governed on with support from former NZ First MPs.

08-15.title: Hobson sails for New Zealand
08-15.text: William Hobson left London with instructions to negotiate a treaty with Māori and establish British authority in New Zealand.

08-15.title: General election of 1987
08-15.text: Labour under David Lange was re-elected, the first time Labour had won a second term since 1946.

08-15.title: Last COVID-19 rules end
08-15.text: The Government removed the last COVID-19 requirements, including isolation for positive cases and masks in healthcare, ending more than three years of pandemic rules.

08-16.title: Atkinson ministry ends
08-16.text: Harry Atkinson's second ministry resigned after the 1884 election, beginning a short period of rapidly changing governments.

08-16.title: Tribunal's interim report on Treaty Principles Bill
08-16.text: The Waitangi Tribunal released an interim report finding the Treaty Principles Bill policy breached the Treaty and urged the Government to abandon it.

08-17.title: Governor refuses full responsible government
08-17.text: When the House met, the acting Governor made clear that ministers would not yet be fully answerable to Parliament, bringing down the FitzGerald ministry.

08-17.title: Election postponed by four weeks
08-17.text: Jacinda Ardern moved the general election from 19 September to 17 October 2020 after a COVID-19 outbreak in Auckland.

08-17.title: Nationwide level 4 lockdown
08-17.text: After a single community case of the Delta variant, the whole country moved to alert level 4 at 11.59pm. Auckland stayed in lockdown for more than 100 days.

08-18.title: Hall-Jones wins Timaru by-election
08-18.text: William Hall-Jones, who in 1906 became the first head of government titled Prime Minister, entered Parliament through a by-election in Timaru.

08-18.title: Tuku Morgan quits New Zealand First
08-18.text: Tuku Morgan left New Zealand First to sit as an independent after the coalition with National collapsed. He later joined the Mauri Pacific party.

08-18.title: Parliament resumes after delayed dissolution
08-18.text: The House returned for limited sittings after the dissolution of Parliament was postponed because of COVID-19.

08-19.title: First same-sex marriages
08-19.text: The Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Act came into force and the first same-sex couples married in New Zealand.

08-19.title: Advance New Zealand deregistered
08-19.text: Advance New Zealand, led by Jami-Lee Ross and Billy Te Kahika at the 2020 election, was deregistered.

08-19.title: Death of Sir Michael Cullen
08-19.text: Sir Michael Cullen, Minister of Finance from 1999 to 2008 and architect of KiwiSaver and the Super Fund, died.

08-20.title: Robert Stout enters Parliament
08-20.text: Future premier Robert Stout won the Caversham by-election.

08-21.title: War Cabinet dissolved
08-21.text: The joint Labour-National War Cabinet was wound up after the end of the Second World War.

08-21.title: 'Smacking' referendum result
08-21.text: Voting closed in the citizens-initiated referendum on parental smacking. About 87 percent voted that a smack should not be a criminal offence, but the law was not changed.

08-21.title: Peter Dunne announces retirement
08-21.text: United Future leader Peter Dunne, MP for Ōhāriu since 1984, announced he would not stand at the 2017 election.

08-22.title: Smacking referendum petition succeeds
08-22.text: The Clerk of the House confirmed that a petition for a citizens-initiated referendum on the 2007 'anti-smacking' law had enough valid signatures.

08-22.title: Ban on foreign home buyers
08-22.text: The Overseas Investment Amendment Act received royal assent, restricting purchases of existing homes to citizens and residents.

08-23.title: Anand Satyanand becomes Governor-General
08-23.text: Sir Anand Satyanand, a former judge and Ombudsman, was sworn in as the first Governor-General of Indian and Pacific descent.

08-23.title: Gaurav Sharma expelled from Labour
08-23.text: Labour expelled Hamilton West MP Gaurav Sharma after he publicly accused the party of bullying. His later resignation forced a by-election.

08-24.title: Adrian Rurawhe elected Speaker
08-24.text: Labour's Adrian Rurawhe became Speaker of the House after Trevor Mallard left Parliament to become ambassador to Ireland.

08-25.title: Massey forms a post-war government
08-25.text: William Massey formed a Reform-only ministry after the wartime coalition with the Liberals ended.

08-26.title: Royal warrant for New Zealand's coat of arms
08-26.text: King George V granted New Zealand its own coat of arms by royal warrant.

08-26.title: Tribunal inquiry into foreshore law changes
