08-26.text: The Waitangi Tribunal began an urgent inquiry into the Government's plan to amend the Marine and Coastal Area Act test for customary title.

08-27.title: Green School funding row
08-27.text: Green co-leader James Shaw faced criticism from within his own party after approving $11.7 million for a private 'Green School' in Taranaki. He later apologised.

08-28.title: Twelve-day ministry falls
08-28.text: The first Stout-Vogel ministry fell after only twelve days, to be followed by an equally short Atkinson ministry.

08-28.title: Bill of Rights Act becomes law
08-28.text: The New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 received royal assent, setting out civil and political rights that courts must consider when interpreting other laws.

08-28.title: Serious Fraud Office investigates NZ First
08-28.text: The Serious Fraud Office began investigating New Zealand First's finances, alongside a Privileges Committee inquiry into donations to Winston Peters.

08-29.title: Peters stands down as minister
08-29.text: Winston Peters stood down from his ministerial roles while the Serious Fraud Office and the Privileges Committee investigated donations to his party.

08-30.title: Parliament prorogued after an extended term
08-30.text: The 26th Parliament ended after a special law had extended its life because of the war. The election followed in September.

08-30.title: Judith Collins resigns as minister
08-30.text: Judith Collins resigned from Cabinet after an email suggested she had tried to undermine a public servant, following the 'Dirty Politics' book.

08-31.title: Death of Norman Kirk
08-31.text: Prime Minister Norman Kirk died in office aged 51. Bill Rowling succeeded him.

08-31.title: Jerry Mateparae becomes Governor-General
08-31.text: Former Chief of Defence Force Sir Jerry Mateparae was sworn in as Governor-General, the second person of Māori descent in the role.

09-01.title: Atkinson becomes premier
09-01.text: Harry Atkinson formed the first of several ministries he would lead over the next 15 years.

09-01.title: Snap election after the waterfront dispute
09-01.text: Sidney Holland's National government won a snap election called after the waterfront dispute, increasing its majority.

09-01.title: Deadline for historical Treaty claims
09-01.text: The last day for lodging historical Treaty of Waitangi claims with the Waitangi Tribunal passed. Claims about events after 1992 can still be made.

09-02.title: Forsaith ministry collapses
09-02.text: Thomas Forsaith's appointed ministry lost the confidence of the House after only three days, as the fight over responsible government continued.

09-02.title: Last sitting day of the 52nd Parliament
09-02.text: Parliament sat for the last time before the delayed 2020 election.

09-02.title: Local Water Done Well law passed
09-02.text: The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act received royal assent, replacing the Three Waters reforms with council-led water plans.

09-03.title: Second Stout-Vogel ministry
09-03.text: Robert Stout and Julius Vogel formed a ministry that lasted three years, ending a month of political instability.

09-03.title: Geoffrey Palmer resigns
09-03.text: Geoffrey Palmer resigned as prime minister seven weeks before the election, and Labour turned to Mike Moore.

09-04.title: Wellington Central MP dies
09-04.text: Robert Fletcher's death led to a by-election won by Labour's Peter Fraser, a future prime minister.

09-04.title: Mike Moore becomes prime minister
09-04.text: Mike Moore was sworn in as prime minister. He lost the election to National 54 days later, the shortest term of any elected prime minister in the 20th century.

09-05.title: Cobham becomes Governor-General
09-05.text: Viscount Cobham was sworn in as Governor-General.

09-05.title: Compulsory superannuation referendum opens
09-05.text: Postal voting began in a referendum on a compulsory retirement savings scheme promoted by Winston Peters. Voters rejected it by about 92 percent.

09-06.title: Bill Rowling becomes prime minister
09-06.text: Bill Rowling was sworn in as prime minister after Norman Kirk's death.

09-06.title: Parliament dissolved for the 2020 election
09-06.text: The 52nd Parliament was dissolved, almost a month later than planned because of COVID-19.

09-06.title: Tāmaki Makaurau by-election
09-06.text: Te Pāti Māori's Oriini Kaipara won the Tāmaki Makaurau by-election held after the death of Takutai Tarsh Kemp.

09-07.title: Māori electorates vote in the 1887 election
09-07.text: Polling in the four Māori electorates was held on 7 September 1887, nearly three weeks before the general electorates.

09-07.title: Clare Curran resigns from Cabinet
09-07.text: Clare Curran resigned all her ministerial portfolios after failing to record meetings and struggling to answer questions in the House.

09-08.title: Upper house passes women's suffrage
09-08.text: The Legislative Council passed the Electoral Bill giving women the vote, 20 votes to 18, after two opponents switched sides in protest at the Premier's tactics.

09-08.title: Parliament dissolved for the 2023 election
09-08.text: The 53rd Parliament was dissolved ahead of the 14 October election.

09-09.title: Dominion proclamation issued
09-09.text: King Edward VII issued the royal proclamation granting New Zealand the title of Dominion, which took effect on 26 September.

09-09.title: Treaty Principles Bill outline released
09-09.text: The Government released a draft outline of ACT's Treaty Principles Bill ahead of its introduction to Parliament in November.

09-10.title: Death of Governor Hobson
09-10.text: William Hobson, who signed the Treaty of Waitangi for the Crown and was New Zealand's first Governor, died in Auckland.

09-10.title: Stafford's third ministry
09-10.text: Edward Stafford returned as premier for a third time, but his ministry lasted only a month.

09-10.title: Writ issued for the 2023 election
09-10.text: The Governor-General issued the writ for the general election, formally starting the 2023 campaign period.

09-11.title: Right of Centre joins National in coalition
09-11.text: The Right of Centre party, formed by former National minister Ross Meurant, entered a coalition with the Bolger government.

09-11.title: Charles III proclaimed King in New Zealand
09-11.text: The accession of King Charles III was proclaimed at Parliament in Wellington, three days after the death of Queen Elizabeth II.

09-12.title: Final Springbok test at Eden Park
09-12.text: The last match of the 1981 tour was played in Auckland amid violent clashes between protesters and police, while a light plane dropped flour bombs on the field.

09-13.title: Atkinson's second ministry
09-13.text: Harry Atkinson reconstituted his government, which went on to see the provinces abolished on 1 November.

09-13.title: First woman elected to Parliament
09-13.text: Elizabeth McCombs won the Lyttelton by-election for Labour, 40 years after women gained the vote.

09-14.title: Social Security Act passed
09-14.text: Parliament passed the Social Security Act, the foundation of the welfare state, including free hospital care and a wider range of benefits.

09-14.title: Māori language petition presented
09-14.text: A petition with more than 30,000 signatures calling for te reo Māori to be taught in schools was presented to Parliament. The date is now Māori Language Day.

09-15.title: First Parliament dissolved
09-15.text: The 1st Parliament was dissolved ahead of the 1855 election.

09-15.title: General election of 1879 ends
09-15.text: Polling in the general electorates ended after nearly three weeks. The new Parliament passed laws for three-year terms and votes for all adult men.

09-16.title: Parliament dissolved for the 1938 election
09-16.text: The 25th Parliament was dissolved, two days after passing the Social Security Act. Labour was re-elected in October.

09-17.title: General election of 2005
09-17.text: Labour narrowly beat National, 41.1 percent to 39.1, and Helen Clark formed a government with the Progressives, New Zealand First and United Future.

09-18.title: Auckland founded as capital
09-18.text: Governor Hobson's officials formally founded Auckland on land offered by Ngāti Whātua chief Apihai Te Kawau. It served as capital until 1865.

09-18.title: Farmers protest water tax in Morrinsville
09-18.text: Federated Farmers rallied against Labour and Green water and pollution tax proposals in Jacinda Ardern's home town, five days before the election.

09-19.title: Women win the vote
09-19.text: Governor Lord Glasgow signed the Electoral Act 1893, making New Zealand the first self-governing country to give all adult women the right to vote in parliamentary elections.

09-19.title: Voters back electoral reform
09-19.text: In an indicative referendum, 84.7 percent voted to change the voting system and 70.5 percent of those chose MMP. A binding vote followed in 1993.

09-20.title: Holyoake becomes prime minister
09-20.text: Sidney Holland stepped down because of ill health and Keith Holyoake became prime minister, less than three months before losing the election.

09-20.title: General election of 2014
09-20.text: John Key's National Party won 47 percent of the vote and a third term. The Internet Mana alliance and Conservative Party failed to enter Parliament.

09-20.title: Meka Whaitiri removed as minister
09-20.text: Jacinda Ardern removed Meka Whaitiri from her ministerial roles after an investigation into an incident with a staff member.

09-21.title: Prostitution Reform Bill introduced
09-21.text: Labour MP Tim Barnett's member's bill to decriminalise sex work was introduced. It became law by one vote in 2003.

09-21.title: Voting-age bill fails first reading
09-21.text: Green MP Golriz Ghahraman's Electoral (Strengthening Democracy) Amendment Bill, which would have lowered the voting age to 16, was defeated at its first reading.

09-22.title: United and Reform form a coalition
09-22.text: The United and Reform parties formed a coalition government under George Forbes to tackle the Depression. The two parties later merged to form National.

09-22.title: France admits the Rainbow Warrior bombing
09-22.text: French Prime Minister Laurent Fabius admitted that French agents had sunk the Rainbow Warrior on government orders.

09-23.title: Referendum on a four-year term
09-23.text: Voters rejected a proposal to extend the parliamentary term from three years to four, by more than two to one. A 1990 referendum had the same result.

09-23.title: General election of 2017
09-23.text: National won the most votes but New Zealand First held the balance of power. Winston Peters chose Labour, making Jacinda Ardern prime minister.

09-24.title: Seventh Parliament opens
09-24.text: The 7th Parliament opened after the 1879 election.

09-25.title: Atkinson's second ministry formed
09-25.text: Harry Atkinson replaced Frederick Whitaker as premier.

09-25.title: Wartime general election
09-25.text: Labour under Peter Fraser was re-elected in an election held two years late because of the war.

09-26.title: General election of 1887
09-26.text: The general electorates voted in an election that returned Harry Atkinson to power during an economic depression.

09-26.title: New Zealand becomes a Dominion
09-26.text: New Zealand changed from a colony to the Dominion of New Zealand, a largely symbolic step marked as Dominion Day.

09-27.title: Jellicoe becomes Governor-General
09-27.text: Admiral Viscount Jellicoe, commander of the British fleet at Jutland, was sworn in as Governor-General.

09-27.title: Denis Blundell becomes Governor-General
09-27.text: Sir Denis Blundell was sworn in as the first New Zealand-resident Governor-General.

09-28.title: Patsy Reddy becomes Governor-General
09-28.text: Dame Patsy Reddy was sworn in as Governor-General, the third woman in the role.

09-29.title: Julius Vogel enters Parliament
09-29.text: Julius Vogel, later premier, took his seat for Dunedin and Suburbs North.

09-30.title: Counter-terrorism law passed
09-30.text: Parliament passed the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Act, criminalising planning a terrorist act, weeks after the Auckland supermarket attack.

10-01.title: GST introduced
10-01.text: The goods and services tax began at 10 percent as part of the Fourth Labour Government's tax reforms. It rose to 12.5 percent in 1989 and 15 percent in 2010.

10-01.title: Parliament dissolved for the 2026 election
10-01.text: The 54th Parliament was dissolved ahead of the general election on 7 November 2026.

10-02.title: War Administration collapses
10-02.text: The joint Labour-National War Administration broke up after a dispute over striking coal miners. The War Cabinet continued.

10-03.title: Parliament dissolved for the 2008 election
10-03.text: The 48th Parliament was dissolved. National under John Key won the election in November.

10-04.title: Official results of the 2014 election
10-04.text: The Electoral Commission released the official 2014 results, including special votes, confirming National's 60 seats.

10-04.title: 'Waka-jumping' law takes effect
10-04.text: The Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act 2018 came into force, letting party leaders remove MPs who leave their party from Parliament. It was a New Zealand First coalition demand.

10-05.title: Blundell ends term as Governor-General
10-05.text: Sir Denis Blundell's term ended. Former prime minister Sir Keith Holyoake succeeded him three weeks later.

10-06.title: Tenth Parliament opens
10-06.text: The 10th Parliament opened after the 1887 election, during the long depression of the 1880s.

10-07.title: Motueka MP dies; Holyoake's first win follows
10-07.text: Independent MP George Black died. Keith Holyoake, a future prime minister, won the resulting Motueka by-election for Reform.

10-07.title: Final results in a hung election
10-07.text: The official 2017 results were released, confirming that New Zealand First held the balance of power. Winston Peters announced his choice twelve days later.

10-08.title: Hall ministry takes office
10-08.text: John Hall became premier. His government introduced three-year parliamentary terms and the vote for all adult men.

10-08.title: Death of Harry Holland
10-08.text: Labour leader Harry Holland died. Michael Joseph Savage replaced him and led Labour to its first election win two years later.

10-09.title: Pubs open until 10pm
10-09.text: Hotel closing time moved from 6pm to 10pm, ending the 'six o'clock swill' three weeks after voters backed the change in a referendum.

10-09.title: Candidate's death forces Port Waikato by-election
10-09.text: The death of ACT's Port Waikato candidate Neil Christensen during advance voting was announced, meaning the electorate contest was cancelled and a by-election held in November.

10-09.title: Oriini Kaipara's maiden speech
10-09.text: Te Pāti Māori's new Tāmaki Makaurau MP Oriini Kaipara gave her maiden speech in Parliament.

10-10.title: Māori Representation Act
10-10.text: The Maori Representation Act created four Māori electorates, giving Māori men the vote for their own seats. Intended as a temporary measure, the seats still exist.

10-10.title: Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975
10-10.text: The Treaty of Waitangi Act, which created the Waitangi Tribunal to hear Māori claims about breaches of the Treaty, became law.

10-11.title: Waterhouse ministry formed
10-11.text: George Waterhouse, a former Premier of South Australia, became premier of New Zealand, the only person to lead governments in two colonies.

10-11.title: Local elections and Māori ward polls
10-11.text: Voters in 42 councils decided in binding polls whether to keep Māori wards, alongside the 2025 local elections. Most voted to remove them.

10-12.title: Savage becomes Labour leader
10-12.text: Michael Joseph Savage was chosen as Labour leader after Harry Holland's death.

10-12.title: Death penalty for murder abolished
10-12.text: Ten National MPs voted with Labour to abolish the death penalty for murder, during debate on the Crimes Bill.

10-12.title: First MMP election
10-12.text: New Zealand held its first election under MMP. New Zealand First won 17 seats and held the balance of power, taking two months to choose National.

10-13.title: Grey ministry takes office
10-13.text: Former governor Sir George Grey became premier, the only person to have held both offices.

10-13.title: Māori land march reaches Parliament
10-13.text: The hīkoi led by Dame Whina Cooper arrived at Parliament after walking the length of the North Island, presenting a petition against further loss of Māori land.

10-14.title: General election of 2023
10-14.text: National won 38 percent and formed a coalition with ACT and New Zealand First. Labour fell to 26.9 percent after six years in office.

10-15.title: General election of 1938
10-15.text: Labour under Michael Joseph Savage was re-elected with an increased share of the vote, a month after passing the Social Security Act.

10-15.title: Supreme Court Act passed
10-15.text: Parliament passed the Supreme Court Act, ending appeals to the Privy Council in London and creating a final court of appeal in Wellington. National, ACT, New Zealand First and United Future opposed it.

10-16.title: Stafford returns as premier
10-16.text: Edward Stafford formed his second ministry after Frederick Weld resigned.

10-16.title: Jami-Lee Ross expelled from National caucus
10-16.text: National expelled Botany MP Jami-Lee Ross after he accused leader Simon Bridges of electoral fraud. He later founded Advance New Zealand.

10-16.title: 'Super Saturday' vaccination day
10-16.text: A national day of COVID-19 vaccinations saw more than 130,000 doses given in one day.

10-17.title: Supreme Court Act receives royal assent
10-17.text: The Supreme Court Act 2003 became law, taking effect on 1 January 2004.

10-17.title: Labour wins an outright majority
10-17.text: Labour won 50 percent of the vote and 65 seats, the first single-party majority under MMP. Voters also backed the End of Life Choice Act and rejected legalising cannabis.

10-18.title: Birth of Sidney Holland
10-18.text: Sidney Holland, the first National Party prime minister (1949-1957), was born in Greendale, Canterbury.

10-18.title: Bill to abolish the country quota
10-18.text: The Labour government introduced a bill to abolish the 'country quota', which had given rural electorates fewer voters than urban ones since 1881.

10-18.title: Gaurav Sharma resigns from Parliament
10-18.text: Expelled Labour MP Gaurav Sharma resigned his Hamilton West seat, forcing a by-election that National won in December.

10-19.title: Peters chooses Labour
10-19.text: Winston Peters announced New Zealand First would form a coalition with Labour, making Jacinda Ardern prime minister with Green support.

10-20.title: Fergusson ends term as Governor-General
10-20.text: Sir Bernard Fergusson, the last British-born Governor-General, finished his term. Sir Arthur Porritt, the first New Zealand-born holder, followed.

10-21.title: Cindy Kiro becomes Governor-General
10-21.text: Dame Cindy Kiro was sworn in as the first Māori woman to be Governor-General.

10-22.title: Darleen Tana expelled from Parliament
10-22.text: Speaker Gerry Brownlee removed independent MP Darleen Tana from Parliament at the Green Party's request, the first use of the 2018 'waka-jumping' law.

10-22.title: Marine and Coastal Area amendment passed
10-22.text: Parliament passed the Government's amendment to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, tightening the test for customary marine title.

10-23.title: Euthanasia law to go to a referendum
10-23.text: Parliament voted 63 to 57 to make the End of Life Choice Bill subject to a binding referendum, a condition set by New Zealand First.

10-24.title: Coalition agreement signed
10-24.text: Labour and New Zealand First signed their coalition agreement, and Labour and the Greens a confidence and supply agreement, two days before Jacinda Ardern was sworn in.

10-25.title: Ardern announces her ministry
10-25.text: The incoming Labour-led government announced its ministers, including Winston Peters as deputy prime minister and Grant Robertson as finance minister.

10-26.title: Holyoake becomes Governor-General
10-26.text: Former prime minister Sir Keith Holyoake was sworn in as Governor-General, a controversial appointment of a serving politician.

10-26.title: Jacinda Ardern sworn in as prime minister
10-26.text: Jacinda Ardern became New Zealand's 40th prime minister at 37, leading a coalition with New Zealand First supported by the Greens.

10-27.title: National wins the 1990 election
10-27.text: Jim Bolger's National Party won a landslide. A referendum held the same day rejected a four-year parliamentary term.

10-28.title: Declaration of Independence
10-28.text: Thirty-four northern chiefs signed He Whakaputanga, the Declaration of the Independence of New Zealand, at Waitangi, asserting Māori sovereignty.

10-28.title: Letters Patent 1983
10-28.text: New Letters Patent defining the office of Governor-General were issued, replacing the 1917 version and removing references to the British Government.

10-29.title: MMP review final report
10-29.text: The Electoral Commission delivered its final report on MMP, recommending a 4 percent threshold and an end to the one-electorate-seat rule. Parliament did not act on it.

10-30.title: Whitaker becomes premier
10-30.text: Frederick Whitaker formed a ministry with William Fox during the Waikato war. It passed the law allowing confiscation of Māori land.

10-31.title: Ardern's first major announcement as PM
10-31.text: Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced the new government's plans, including a ban on foreign buyers of existing homes.

11-01.title: Provinces abolished
11-01.text: New Zealand's nine provincial governments were abolished, leaving central government and local councils.

11-01.title: Labour and Greens sign cooperation agreement
11-01.text: Labour, with a majority of its own, signed a cooperation agreement giving the Greens two ministers outside Cabinet.

11-02.title: Bolger government takes office
11-02.text: Jim Bolger was sworn in as prime minister, beginning nine years of National government.

11-02.title: Ardern's second-term Cabinet announced
11-02.text: Jacinda Ardern announced a new Cabinet, with Grant Robertson as deputy prime minister and the most diverse ministry to date.

11-03.title: Waikato-Tainui settlement becomes law
11-03.text: Queen Elizabeth II signed the Waikato Raupatu Claims Settlement Act in Wellington, including a Crown apology for the 1860s confiscations.

11-03.title: Final results of the 2023 election
11-03.text: Official results confirmed National and ACT needed New Zealand First to govern. Coalition talks took another three weeks.

11-04.title: General election of 1925
11-04.text: Gordon Coates led the Reform Party to a landslide win on the slogan 'Coats off with Coates'.

11-04.title: The Opportunities Party launched
11-04.text: Economist Gareth Morgan launched The Opportunities Party (TOP).

11-05.title: Invasion of Parihaka
11-05.text: About 1,600 troops led by Native Minister John Bryce entered the peaceful Māori settlement of Parihaka, arrested its leaders Te Whiti and Tohu, and destroyed homes.

11-05.title: Pike River Royal Commission reports
11-05.text: The Royal Commission on the Pike River mine disaster blamed the company's failures and weak regulation. Labour Minister Kate Wilkinson resigned that portfolio the same day.

11-06.title: Voters choose MMP
11-06.text: In a binding referendum held with the general election, 53.9 percent voted to replace first-past-the-post with MMP. National narrowly won the election.

11-06.title: Death of Rod Donald
11-06.text: Green co-leader Rod Donald died suddenly aged 48, days before the new Parliament was sworn in.

11-06.title: Ardern sworn in for a second term
11-06.text: Jacinda Ardern and her new ministers were sworn in after Labour's majority win.

11-07.title: 52nd Parliament opens
11-07.text: The new Parliament met and elected Trevor Mallard as Speaker.

11-07.title: Zero Carbon Act passed
11-07.text: Parliament passed the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act with support from all parties except ACT, setting a net-zero target for 2050.

11-07.title: General election of 2026
11-07.text: Election day for the 55th Parliament. Advance voting opens in the weeks before.

11-08.title: National wins the 2008 election
11-08.text: John Key led National to victory, ending nine years of Labour government under Helen Clark.

11-08.title: State Opening of Parliament
11-08.text: The Governor-General read the speech from the throne setting out the new Labour-led government's programme.

11-09.title: Bernard Fergusson becomes Governor-General
11-09.text: Sir Bernard Fergusson, whose father and both grandfathers had also been Governors of New Zealand, was sworn in.

11-10.title: First Deputy Speaker appointed
11-10.text: Parliament appointed its first Deputy Speaker, replacing the old role of Chairman of Committees.

11-10.title: Shane Reti becomes National deputy leader
11-10.text: National MPs elected Shane Reti as deputy leader under Judith Collins after the party's 2020 election defeat.

11-11.title: Awatere Huata declared an independent
11-11.text: ACT list MP Donna Awatere Huata was formally declared an independent after her suspension from the party, setting up the first use of the party-hopping law.

11-12.title: Te Whiti and Tohu charged
11-12.text: Parihaka leaders Te Whiti and Tohu appeared in court in New Plymouth charged with sedition. They were held without trial until 1883.

11-12.title: Crown apology to abuse in care survivors
11-12.text: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon delivered a formal apology in Parliament to survivors of abuse in state and faith-based care.

11-13.title: The Queen opens Parliament
11-13.text: Queen Elizabeth II opened a session of Parliament during her 1986 visit.

11-13.title: End of Life Choice Act passed
11-13.text: Parliament passed David Seymour's End of Life Choice Act, subject to a referendum. Voters approved it in 2020 and it took effect in November 2021.

11-13.title: Zero Carbon Act receives royal assent
11-13.text: The Zero Carbon Act became law, setting up the Climate Change Commission and emissions budgets.

11-14.title: General election of 1928
11-14.text: Sir Joseph Ward's United Party won enough seats to form a government, ending Reform's 16 years in office.

11-14.title: Haka interrupts Treaty Principles Bill vote
11-14.text: Te Pāti Māori MP Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke tore up a copy of the bill and led a haka during the first reading vote, bringing the House to a halt. The bill passed its first reading 68 to 55.

11-15.title: First MP 'named' by the Speaker
11-15.text: Julius Vogel became the first MP to be named by the Speaker, the House's formal disciplinary step, for comments about another member.

11-15.title: Birth of Bill Rowling
11-15.text: Bill Rowling, prime minister from 1974 to 1975 after Norman Kirk's death, was born in Motueka.

11-15.title: Vaccine mandates take effect for health and education
11-15.text: COVID-19 vaccination became compulsory for workers in health, disability, education, corrections, defence, fire and police roles.

11-16.title: Charter creates the Colony of New Zealand
11-16.text: The British Government issued the charter making New Zealand a separate colony from May 1841, with a Governor and an appointed Legislative Council.

11-16.title: Writ returned for the 2023 election
11-16.text: The writ confirming the elected members of the 54th Parliament was returned to the Clerk of the House.

11-17.title: General election of 1908
11-17.text: Joseph Ward's Liberals won the first election held under the second-ballot system, which was used only in 1908 and 1911.

11-18.title: George Grey takes office as Governor
11-18.text: Sir George Grey began the first of his two terms as Governor, during the Northern War.

11-18.title: Andrew Little becomes Labour leader
11-18.text: Andrew Little narrowly won Labour's leadership contest after the party's 2014 defeat under David Cunliffe.

11-19.title: John Key sworn in as prime minister
11-19.text: John Key became prime minister, leading a National government supported by ACT, United Future and the Māori Party.

11-19.title: Pike River mine explosion
11-19.text: An explosion at the Pike River coal mine on the West Coast trapped 29 men, who died. The disaster led to a royal commission and a new workplace safety regulator.

11-19.title: Hīkoi mō te Tiriti reaches Parliament
11-19.text: Tens of thousands of people marched on Parliament at the end of a nine-day hīkoi against the Treaty Principles Bill, one of the largest protests in New Zealand history.

11-20.title: Paul Reeves becomes Governor-General
11-20.text: Archbishop Sir Paul Reeves was sworn in as the first Governor-General of Māori descent.

11-20.title: First flag referendum opens
11-20.text: Postal voting began in the first of two referendums on changing the national flag. A silver fern design was chosen to go up against the current flag in March 2016.

11-21.title: Statute of Westminster bill passes
11-21.text: Parliament passed the Statute of Westminster Adoption Bill at its third reading. It received royal assent four days later.

11-21.title: Ngāi Tahu deed of settlement signed
11-21.text: Prime Minister Jim Bolger and Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu signed a deed settling the iwi's claims, worth $170 million. The settlement Act followed in 1998.

11-21.title: Supreme Court rules on the voting age
11-21.text: The Supreme Court declared that setting the voting age at 18 rather than 16 was inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act, prompting the Government to propose a bill for local elections.

11-22.title: Rainbow Warrior agents sentenced
11-22.text: Two French agents pleaded guilty to manslaughter over the Rainbow Warrior bombing and were sentenced to ten years in prison.

11-23.title: Don Brash resigns as National leader
11-23.text: Don Brash resigned as National leader just before the release of Nicky Hager's book The Hollow Men, based on leaked party emails.

11-24.title: Foreshore and Seabed Act becomes law
11-24.text: The Foreshore and Seabed Act received royal assent, vesting the foreshore and seabed in the Crown. The dispute led to the founding of the Māori Party. It was repealed in 2011.

11-24.title: Vaccine mandate law passed
11-24.text: Parliament passed the COVID-19 Response (Vaccinations) Legislation Act, allowing employers to dismiss workers who refused vaccination in mandated roles.

11-24.title: Three-party coalition agreed
11-24.text: National, ACT and New Zealand First signed coalition agreements, with Winston Peters and David Seymour to share the deputy prime ministership.

11-25.title: Statute of Westminster adopted
11-25.text: Parliament passed the Statute of Westminster Adoption Act, giving New Zealand full power to make its own laws independent of Britain.

11-25.title: Judith Collins removed as National leader
11-25.text: National MPs voted no confidence in Judith Collins after she demoted Simon Bridges. Christopher Luxon was elected leader five days later.

11-25.title: Port Waikato by-election
11-25.text: National's Andrew Bayly won the Port Waikato by-election, held because an ACT candidate died during the general election campaign.

11-26.title: Holland replaces Hamilton as National leader
11-26.text: Sidney Holland took over from Adam Hamilton as leader of the National Party. He became prime minister in 1949.

11-26.title: Election and MMP referendum
11-26.text: National won a second term under John Key. In a referendum held the same day, 57.8 percent voted to keep MMP.

11-26.title: State Opening of the 53rd Parliament
11-26.text: The Governor-General opened the new Parliament following Labour's majority win. Te Pāti Māori MPs walked out in protest at speaking-time rules.

11-27.title: Labour wins the 1999 election
11-27.text: Helen Clark's Labour Party won the election and formed a coalition with the Alliance, ending nine years of National government.

11-27.title: John Key becomes National leader
11-27.text: John Key was elected leader of the National Party after Don Brash's resignation. He led the party to three election wins.

11-27.title: Christopher Luxon sworn in as prime minister
11-27.text: Christopher Luxon became the 42nd prime minister, leading a National-ACT-New Zealand First coalition.

11-28.title: Women vote for the first time
11-28.text: More than 90,000 women voted in the general election, ten weeks after winning the right to do so.

11-28.title: General election of 1981
11-28.text: Robert Muldoon's National Party won a third term with a one-seat majority, despite winning fewer votes than Labour.

11-28.title: COVID-19 Royal Commission reports
11-28.text: The Royal Commission into the COVID-19 response released its first report, broadly endorsing the early response while criticising the length of later lockdowns.

11-29.title: General election of 1969
11-29.text: Keith Holyoake's National Party won a fourth consecutive term, the first election with a voting age of 20.

11-29.title: Muldoon wins the 1975 election
11-29.text: Robert Muldoon led National to a landslide victory over Bill Rowling's Labour government.

11-29.title: Goff and King step down
11-29.text: Labour leader Phil Goff and deputy Annette King announced their resignations after the 2011 election defeat.

11-30.title: National wins the 1949 election
11-30.text: Sidney Holland's National Party defeated Labour, ending 14 years of Labour government.

11-30.title: Laila Harré steps down as Alliance leader
11-30.text: Laila Harré resigned as leader of the Alliance and was replaced by Matt McCarten.

11-30.title: Christopher Luxon elected National leader
11-30.text: National MPs chose Christopher Luxon as leader with Nicola Willis as deputy, replacing Judith Collins.

12-01.title: Legislative Council sits for the last time
12-01.text: New Zealand's appointed upper house held its final sitting. Its abolition took effect on 1 January 1951.

12-01.title: First New Zealand-born Governor-General
12-01.text: Sir Arthur Porritt, an Olympic medallist and surgeon, was sworn in as the first New Zealand-born Governor-General.

12-01.title: Alliance formed
12-01.text: NewLabour, the Greens, the Democrats and Mana Motuhake formally agreed to form the Alliance, led by Jim Anderton.

12-02.title: General election of 1931
12-02.text: The United-Reform coalition won the Depression-era election against a rising Labour Party.

12-02.title: Norrie becomes Governor-General
12-02.text: Lord Norrie was sworn in as Governor-General.

12-02.title: First citizens-initiated referendum
12-02.text: The first referendum under the Citizens Initiated Referenda Act asked about firefighter numbers. Turnout was low and the result was not binding.

12-03.title: Mount Roskill by-election
12-03.text: Labour's Michael Wood won the Mount Roskill by-election after Phil Goff became Mayor of Auckland.

12-03.title: 'Traffic light' system replaces lockdowns
12-03.text: The COVID-19 Protection Framework came into force, ending alert levels and Auckland's long lockdown, with vaccine passes used for many venues.

12-04.title: General election of 1896
12-04.text: Richard Seddon's Liberals were returned to power.

12-04.title: Paid parental leave extended
12-04.text: A law extending paid parental leave to 26 weeks by 2020 received royal assent, one of the new government's first measures.

12-05.title: General election of 1890
12-05.text: The 1890 election brought the Liberals to power and is often seen as the start of party politics in New Zealand.

12-05.title: John Key announces his resignation
12-05.text: Prime Minister John Key unexpectedly announced he would step down after eight years, saying he had nothing left in the tank. Bill English succeeded him.

12-05.title: 54th Parliament opens
12-05.text: The new Parliament met and elected Gerry Brownlee as Speaker. Te Pāti Māori held protests around the country the same day.

12-06.title: First Labour government sworn in
12-06.text: Michael Joseph Savage became prime minister, beginning 14 years of Labour government that built the welfare state.

12-06.title: Bill English stands for the leadership
12-06.text: Deputy Prime Minister Bill English announced he would seek the National leadership after John Key's resignation. He was confirmed six days later.

12-06.title: State Opening of the 54th Parliament
12-06.text: The Governor-General delivered the speech from the throne for the National-led coalition government.

12-07.title: General election of 1911
12-07.text: Voting in the 1911 election left the Liberals without a clear majority. Within months Reform under William Massey took power.

12-07.title: General election of 1922
12-07.text: William Massey's Reform government lost its majority but stayed in office with independent support.

12-08.title: Norman Kirk becomes prime minister
12-08.text: Norman Kirk was sworn in as prime minister after Labour's 1972 election win, ending 12 years of National government.

12-08.title: Jenny Shipley becomes first woman prime minister
12-08.text: Jenny Shipley was sworn in as prime minister after forcing Jim Bolger's resignation as National leader.

12-09.title: General election of 1881
12-09.text: The 1881 election was the first held with the vote for all adult men and the first after the Parihaka invasion.

12-09.title: Supreme Court Bill introduced
12-09.text: Attorney-General Margaret Wilson introduced the bill to end appeals to the Privy Council and create a Supreme Court of New Zealand.

12-09.title: Civil Union Act passed
12-09.text: Parliament passed the Civil Union Act 65 votes to 55, allowing same-sex and opposite-sex couples to form civil unions from April 2005.

12-10.title: Ward returns as prime minister
12-10.text: Sir Joseph Ward's United Party took office after Gordon Coates lost a confidence vote, 16 years after Ward's first term ended.

12-10.title: Helen Clark sworn in as prime minister
12-10.text: Helen Clark became prime minister, leading a Labour-Alliance coalition with Green support. She governed for nine years.

12-10.title: Hamilton West by-election
12-10.text: National's Tama Potaka won the Hamilton West by-election after former Labour MP Gaurav Sharma resigned.

12-11.title: Parliament Buildings destroyed by fire
12-11.text: Fire destroyed most of the wooden Parliament Buildings in Wellington. The present Parliament House opened in 1922.

12-11.title: Muldoon's third ministry sworn in
12-11.text: Robert Muldoon's ministers were sworn in for a third term after the one-seat election win of November 1981.

12-11.title: National signs agreement with Māori Party
12-11.text: National and the Māori Party renewed their confidence-and-supply agreement after the 2011 election.

12-12.title: Walter Nash becomes prime minister
12-12.text: Walter Nash was sworn in as prime minister of the Second Labour Government, which lasted a single term.

12-12.title: Muldoon becomes prime minister
12-12.text: Robert Muldoon was sworn in as prime minister after National's 1975 landslide. He held office until 1984.

12-12.title: Bill English becomes prime minister
12-12.text: Bill English was sworn in as prime minister, with Paula Bennett as deputy, following John Key's resignation.

12-13.title: First National government takes office
12-13.text: Sidney Holland was sworn in as prime minister, the first from the National Party.

12-13.title: Constitution Act 1986 passed
12-13.text: Parliament unanimously passed the Constitution Act, which replaced the 1852 Act and tidied up New Zealand's constitutional rules. It took effect on 1 January 1987.

12-13.title: David Shearer becomes Labour leader
12-13.text: David Shearer took over as Labour leader after Phil Goff's resignation, defeating David Cunliffe in a caucus vote.

12-14.title: Fair Pay Agreements repealed
12-14.text: The coalition government repealed the Fair Pay Agreements system for sector-wide bargaining introduced by Labour in 2022.

12-15.title: Georgina Beyer announces retirement
12-15.text: Georgina Beyer, the world's first openly transgender MP, announced she would leave Parliament.

12-15.title: Housing intensification law passed
12-15.text: Parliament passed the Resource Management (Enabling Housing Supply) Amendment Act, agreed between Labour and National, allowing three homes of three storeys on most urban sites.

12-16.title: Māori Loans Affair exposed
12-16.text: Opposition MP Winston Peters revealed that officials had sought an unauthorised overseas loan for Māori development, embarrassing the Lange government.

12-17.title: General election and liquor referendum
12-17.text: Voters re-elected William Massey's Reform government and voted in a referendum that narrowly kept the sale of alcohol legal.

12-17.title: Muldoon leaves Parliament
12-17.text: Former prime minister Sir Robert Muldoon resigned as MP for Tamaki after 31 years, triggering a by-election.

12-17.title: Medicinal cannabis law passed
12-17.text: The Misuse of Drugs (Medicinal Cannabis) Amendment Act received royal assent, allowing wider access to medicinal cannabis products.

12-18.title: Electoral Finance Bill passes
12-18.text: Parliament passed the Electoral Finance Bill 63 votes to 57 after months of protest. It was signed into law the next day and repealed in 2009.

12-18.title: Cannabis referendum announced
12-18.text: The Government announced a referendum on legalising recreational cannabis, held with the 2020 election. Voters narrowly rejected the proposal.

12-18.title: Rua Kēnana pardoned
12-18.text: Parliament passed a law pardoning the Tūhoe prophet Rua Kēnana, who was arrested in a 1916 police raid, as part of a Treaty settlement.

12-19.title: Electoral Finance Act signed into law
12-19.text: The Governor-General signed the Electoral Finance Act, tightening rules on election spending and third-party advertising. It was repealed in 2009.

12-20.title: General election of 1875-76 begins
12-20.text: Polling began in a general election spread over six weeks, the last before the provinces were abolished.

12-20.title: Māori electorates vote in the 1893 election
12-20.text: Polling in the four Māori electorates was held three weeks after the general electorates, with Māori women voting for the first time.

12-20.title: 50th Parliament sworn in
12-20.text: Members of the 50th Parliament were sworn in and Lockwood Smith was re-elected Speaker.

12-21.title: Gun buy-back ends
12-21.text: The six-month firearms buy-back that followed the Christchurch attacks closed, with more than 56,000 prohibited firearms handed in.

12-22.title: George Grey elected for Auckland
12-22.text: Former governor Sir George Grey was declared elected unopposed in the two-member City of Auckland seat during the 1875-76 general election.

12-22.title: Party-hopping bill introduced
12-22.text: The new Labour-Alliance government introduced the Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Bill to stop MPs who leave their party keeping their seats. It became law in 2001.

12-23.title: The Queen arrives in New Zealand
12-23.text: Queen Elizabeth II arrived in Auckland, the first reigning monarch to visit New Zealand, for a tour that included opening Parliament.

12-24.title: Death of Speaker Roy Jack
12-24.text: Sir Roy Jack, Speaker of the House, died in office. Richard Harrison replaced him.

12-25.title: Tūrangawaewae marae's first hui
12-25.text: The first gathering was held at Tūrangawaewae in Ngāruawāhia, which Te Puea Hērangi developed as the home of the Kīngitanga, the Māori King movement.

12-26.title: Moutoa monument unveiled in Whanganui
12-26.text: A monument to Māori who fought for the Crown at Moutoa Island was unveiled at what is now Pākaitore (Moutoa Gardens), later the site of a 79-day occupation in 1995.

12-27.title: Birth of Geoff Simmons
12-27.text: Geoff Simmons, economist and leader of The Opportunities Party from 2018 to 2022, was born.

12-28.title: Christchurch MP resigns
12-28.text: Richard Packer resigned as MP for the Town of Christchurch, leading to a by-election won by Henry Sewell, New Zealand's first premier.

12-29.title: Birth of Marama Davidson
12-29.text: Marama Davidson, Green Party co-leader since 2018, was born.

12-29.title: Death of Sir Michael Hardie Boys
12-29.text: Sir Michael Hardie Boys, Governor-General from 1996 to 2001 and the first to oversee government formation under MMP, died aged 92.

12-30.title: The Queen visits Tūrangawaewae
12-30.text: Queen Elizabeth II made a brief visit to Tūrangawaewae marae, hosted by the Māori King Korokī, during her first tour of New Zealand.

12-30.title: Birth of Bill English
12-30.text: Bill English, prime minister from 2016 to 2017 and Minister of Finance from 2008 to 2016, was born in Lumsden, Southland.

12-31.title: George Grey's first term as Governor ends
12-31.text: Sir George Grey left office after eight years as Governor, having overseen the Constitution Act that created Parliament.
